question: Universal Containers (UC) operates worldwide, with offices in more than 100 regions in 10 different countries, and has established a very complex Role Hierarchy to control data visibility. In the new fiscal year, UC is planning to reorganize the roles and reassign account owners. Which feature should an architect recommend to avoid problems with this operation?
optionA: Partition data using Divisions
optionB: Skinny table
optionC: Deferred Sharing Recalculation
explanation:
Deferred Sharing Recalculation is the feature to recommend. Reorganizing roles and reassigning many account owners triggers a massive sharing recalculation that can degrade performance and cause lock errors; Deferred Sharing Recalculation lets the admin suspend automatic group-membership and sharing-rule processing during the bulk change and process it afterward, in one pass.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Partition data using Divisions) — Divisions only partition data for queries and reports; they do nothing to reduce the sharing recalculation a role reorganization triggers.
Option B (Skinny table) — a skinny table is a read-performance structure for reports and list views; it does not touch group membership or share-row maintenance.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_defer_sharing_calculations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_tools_deferred_sharing_maintenance.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) delivers training and courses to students and companies. UC is implementing a Salesforce Customer Community for its students granting them a Customer Community license. As part of the community requirements, UC asked to give students access to cases that are related to their account in the UC community. What is the optimum sharing technique to achieve these requirements?
optionA: Use Apex sharing to share cases with the students.
optionB: Create a sharing rule to share cases with the students.
optionC: Create a sharing set to share cases with the students.
explanation:
Creating a sharing set to share cases with the students is the optimum technique. Customer Community licenses have no roles, so role-hierarchy and sharing-rule approaches do not apply. A Sharing Set is the purpose-built, declarative mechanism that grants community users access to records associated with their own Account or Contact via the lookup, which is exactly cases-by-account.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex sharing to share cases with the students) — it could work, but it is custom code and far more maintenance than the declarative Sharing Set designed for this case.
Option B (a sharing rule to share cases with the students) — sharing rules target roles, groups and territories; Customer Community users have no roles, so a rule cannot be aimed at them per account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is implementing Sales Cloud. During the final quarter of the financial year, sales managers help each other close deals. They requested a solution in Salesforce to allow them to share opportunities with other sales managers from different teams as needed. They also requested that sharing deals should expire automatically 2 weeks after the new fiscal year starts. Which proposed solution meets the requirements?
optionA: Apex sharing to share opportunities with sales managers
optionB: Scheduled Apex job to remove access
optionC: Sharing rules to share opportunities with sales managers
explanation:
Apex sharing to share opportunities with sales managers, plus a scheduled Apex job to remove access, meets both requirements. Ad-hoc, as-needed sharing among managers from different teams has no fixed role or criteria pattern, so it requires programmatic Apex managed sharing to grant access on demand; the scheduled job then deletes those share rows two weeks into the new fiscal year to satisfy the auto-expiry requirement.
Why the other option is wrong:
Option C (Sharing rules to share opportunities with sales managers) — sharing rules are owner- or criteria-based and can neither target arbitrary peers chosen deal by deal nor expire automatically on a date.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://architect.salesforce.com/fundamentals/platform-sharing-architecture

question: At Universal Containers, there's a team of auditors distributed throughout the organization that all need access to high-value opportunities. With a Private sharing model, which option should an architect recommend when designing a solution for this requirement?
optionA: Create a criteria-based sharing rule to grant a public group access to high-value opportunities.
optionB: Add the auditors to the default Opportunity Team.
optionC: Put the auditors at the highest level of the Role Hierarchy.
explanation:
Creating a criteria-based sharing rule to grant a public group access to high-value opportunities is the recommendation. With a Private model, a criteria-based rule keyed on the high-value flag grants the auditors (collected in a public group) access regardless of where they sit in the org.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Add the auditors to the default Opportunity Team) — manual, per-record and per-owner, so it does not scale to a distributed audit team and misses every opportunity whose owner did not add them.
Option C (Put the auditors at the highest level of the Role Hierarchy) — that would expose all opportunities, not just the high-value ones, and misuses the hierarchy for a group that is not management.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a custom Lightning component with an Apex class to display shipment information (custom object, Private organization-wide default). UC sales managers are complaining about two important points: Shipment records that belong to their teams can be seen by other users. Shipment amount should be visible only by managers, but sales reps are able to view it. Which feature did the development team miss that is causing the problems?
optionA: Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility.
optionB: Use isAccessible() method in Apex classes to check field accessibility.
optionC: Use runAs in test class to enforce user permissions and field level permissions.
explanation:
Using the isAccessible() method in Apex classes to check field accessibility is the keyed answer, and of the three options it is the only one that names a real mechanism. Enforce Object and Field Permissions documents Schema.DescribeFieldResult.isAccessible() as the check for a field's read access, so calling it before returning the shipment amount is what keeps that field away from sales reps.
Be careful about the first complaint in the stem, though: isAccessible() does nothing about it. Records visible to the wrong users is a record-access problem, fixed by the class's sharing declaration (or by running the query in user mode), not by a field describe. No option offered here addresses it.
One version note worth carrying: how much Apex enforces by default has moved. In API version 66.0 and earlier Apex runs in system mode by default; in 67.0 and later it runs in user mode, so the running user's permissions and field-level security are enforced unless the code opts into system mode. An @AuraEnabled class that declares no sharing keyword has long used an implicit "with sharing".
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes) — "isShareable" is not an Apex construct; there is no such keyword or describe method.
Option C (Use runAs in test class to enforce permissions) — runAs is a testing method that switches user context inside a test; it enforces nothing at runtime for real users.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_perms_enforcing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-security.html
_cat: Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation implied isAccessible() fixed both complaints in the stem; it addresses only the field-level one. Nothing in the option set fixes the record-visibility complaint, which needs a sharing declaration or a user-mode query — so the item is defective as printed.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is in a legal dispute regarding several orders. UC has found out these records were removed from the system. The VP of Sales has asked to ensure this cannot happen in the future. Which approach should meet this requirement?
optionA: Change the Record Type/Page Layout assignment for Orders to be Read-Only.
optionB: Remove the Delete button from the Order Page Layout.
optionC: Remove Order Delete permission from profiles and permission sets.
explanation:
Removing the Order Delete permission from profiles and permission sets is the approach that meets the requirement. Deleting records is governed by object-level CRUD on profiles and permission sets, so removing Delete is the only reliable way to prevent deletion through any channel, including list views, the API and Apex.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Change the Record Type/Page Layout assignment to Read-Only) — record types and page layouts do not control the delete operation at all; a read-only layout still leaves Delete available through other paths.
Option B (Remove the Delete button from the Order Page Layout) — this merely hides the button in one UI and does not stop list-view, API or Apex deletes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A junior account manager owns an account and creates a new opportunity to manage a complex deal. She needs the help of the product specialist and solution engineer. Given the size of this deal, she knows the account is likely to be reassigned to a senior account manager in the near future. What is the optimal way for the junior account manager to share the opportunity, given the private sharing model?
optionA: Manual share on the opportunity
optionB: Manual share on the account
optionC: Opportunity Team
explanation:
An Opportunity Team is the optimal way to share the opportunity. It is the durable way to bring the product specialist and solution engineer onto this deal, and the mechanisms differ precisely on what happens at a transfer: "User managed sharing is removed when the record owner changes", and Salesforce walks through the same behaviour under the hood — "When a record owner changes, Salesforce deletes its associated sharing rows with Manual row causes." Team-based access is not a manual share and is not swept away with them.
That matters here because the junior account manager expects the deal to move. Once the opportunity is reassigned, a manual share on it is gone and the specialists silently lose access; the team survives the handover.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Manual share on the opportunity) — works today but is deleted the moment the opportunity's owner changes, which the stem says is likely.
Option B (Manual share on the account) — sharing the account grants nothing on the opportunity; access flows implicitly from child up to parent, not from parent down to child.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.salesteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/latest/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_record_access_under_the_hood.pdf

question: A sales coach at Universal Containers wants to create and share a report folder with other sales coaches. Which two permissions are required to accomplish this?
optionA: Create Report Folders and manage Reports in Public Folders
optionB: Create and customize Reports and Report Folders
optionC: Manage Reports in Public Folders and edit My Reports
explanation:
Create Report Folders and Manage Reports in Public Folders are the two permissions required. Creating a report folder requires the "Create Report Folders" permission, and sharing or managing what is inside a public report folder requires "Manage Reports in Public Folders"; together they let the coach build and share the folder. This corrects the source, which selected the report-building option rather than the folder-management pair.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Create and customize Reports and Report Folders) — covers building and customizing reports, not the folder-sharing administration this scenario needs.
Option C (Manage Reports in Public Folders and edit My Reports) — "edit My Reports" concerns the user's private reports and does nothing to create or share a folder.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.analytics_sharing_permissions.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.access_report_folders.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses 75,000 distributors that have close to 1 million total users. Distributors need opportunities assigned to the distributor for delivery. What license recommendation will meet distributor needs?
optionA: Sales Cloud
optionB: Customer Community Plus
optionC: Partner Community
optionD: Customer Community
explanation:
Partner Community is the license recommendation. Distributors that need opportunities assigned to them for delivery are channel partners performing sales and CRM work, which requires Partner Community because it supports Opportunities and partner roles. The one-million-user volume is supported under Partner Community licensing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales Cloud) — a full internal license, priced and intended for employees, not for a million external distributor users.
Option B (Customer Community Plus) — oriented to support and self-service; it adds roles and reports but does not cover Opportunities for channel sales.
Option D (Customer Community) — lacks roles and the full CRM objects, so it cannot carry opportunity assignment to distributors.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers would like to control access to records and objects according to the following business requirements: Sales users can view all account records but only edit their own records. Sales managers can view all account records but only edit records of their team. Service users can view all account records that are not marked with a RecordType of Prospect. Which organization-wide default configuration should an architect recommend to fulfill these requirements?
optionA: Public Read Write
optionB: Public Read/Transfer
optionC: Private
explanation:
Private is the organization-wide default to recommend. Only a Private OWD lets you start from no access and layer the differentiated rules: edit-own for sales users, edit-team for managers via role hierarchy, and record-type-based exclusions for service users. A restrictive baseline is the prerequisite for all the layered grants.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Public Read Write) — grants every user edit on every account, so "edit only your own or your team's" cannot be enforced.
Option B (Public Read/Transfer) — still opens read to everyone and adds transfer; it cannot hide Prospect records from service users or restrict editing to owners and teams.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a team that analyzes customer orders looking for fraud. This team needs access to Invoice records (custom object, Private organization-wide default). UC has complex rules to control users' access. The architect recommended using Apex managed sharing to meet these requirements. Which recommendation should a developer consider when implementing the changes?
optionA: Use "Without Sharing" keyword to make sure record visibility will be considered.
optionB: Use "With Sharing" keyword to enforce Field-Level Security.
optionC: Use runAs system method to test different users accessing these records.
explanation:
Using the runAs system method to test different users accessing these records is the recommendation. Apex managed sharing inserts share rows in system context, so the safeguard against improper access is rigorous testing; runAs() in test methods validates that each user sees only the records intended.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Use "Without Sharing" keyword to make sure record visibility will be considered) — without sharing does the opposite of what the option claims: it ignores the user's record access and would worsen the risk.
Option B (Use "With Sharing" keyword to enforce Field-Level Security) — with sharing enforces record-level sharing only; it does not enforce field-level security, so the option's stated rationale is incorrect.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_runas.htm

question: Which functionality does the system method "runAs()" verify when writing test methods?
optionA: Enforcement of a user's record sharing
optionB: Enforcement of a user's Field-Level Security
optionC: Enforcement of a user's permissions
explanation:
Enforcement of a user's record sharing is the answer this item wants, and it is the answer the exam keys. Read the current documentation carefully, though, because the item is broken against it: Using the runAs Method says that after the user context switches, "the user's sharing rules and object-level and field-level permissions are enforced", and repeats it — "The user's sharing rules and object-level and field-level permissions are enforced within a runAs block, regardless of the sharing mode (with sharing or without sharing) of the test class."
So all three options describe something runAs enforces today. The reason A is still the best answer is that record sharing is the thing runAs exists for: outside a runAs block Apex generally runs in system mode, where object- and field-level permissions of the running user are not taken into account, and runAs is the only way a test can put itself in a specific user's record-access shoes.
If you need to assert object or field permissions in code rather than in a test, that is a separate mechanism — user-mode database operations, or the Schema describe methods isAccessible, isCreateable and isUpdateable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Enforcement of a user's Field-Level Security) — the legacy exam reading is that runAs does not verify FLS; current documentation says it is enforced inside the block, so this is defensible today but not the keyed answer.
Option C (Enforcement of a user's permissions) — likewise true under current documentation, but not what the exam keys; the item is defective as printed and record sharing remains the intended answer.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_runas.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_perms_enforcing.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands, but the old explanation stated that runAs "does not enforce the user's object permissions or Field-Level Security" and that "under runAs, Apex still executes in system mode for CRUD and FLS". The Apex Developer Guide says the opposite: object-level and field-level permissions are enforced inside a runAs block. Treat the item as defective — all three options are true of runAs as currently documented.

question: A consulting company uses the Salesforce mobile app for its field consultants and uses Case object to track customer specific consulting done by field consultants. The company also has a large number of customer service representatives who takes calls from customers on company issued desktops, and uses case object to track customer issues and grievances. The company would like to capture images of customer site captured by field consultants while they are editing the case record during customer site visit. The Director of IT wants to minimize customization and promote reuseability of code artifacts wherever possible. What recommendations should an architect give to the company to implement the image capture requirement, while ensuring customer that the service rep can continue to use same lightning pages they were trained to use?
optionA: Use Lightning Component as an override for "Edit" action on mobile view allowing image capture feature. No Change required for desktop users.
optionB: Use Lightning Component as an override for "Edit" action on lightning experience allowing image capture feature. Detect the form factor of the device and redirect the user to the default not overridden view.
optionC: Create a separate button "Edit in Mobile", which opens a custom lightning component that will allow field consultants to add an image. No change required for desktop users.
explanation:
Using a Lightning Component as an override for the "Edit" action on the mobile view, with no change required for desktop users, is the recommendation. Overriding the Edit action only on the mobile view adds image capture for field consultants while leaving desktop service reps on the standard Lightning pages they were trained on, maximizing reuse and minimizing customization. Assign Action Overrides lets you specify the override option for each user experience separately.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Override "Edit" on Lightning Experience and redirect by form factor) — introduces form-factor detection and redirect complexity, and changes the desktop experience the service reps were trained on.
Option C (Create a separate "Edit in Mobile" button) — a separate custom button is extra customization the Director explicitly wanted to avoid, and it leaves the standard Edit action without image capture.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.assign_action_overrides.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.standard_actions_overrides.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields

question: Universal Containers requested to leverage Lightning Web Components (LWC) to improve support reps' user experience. LWC will be used as view layer, and Apex classes will have the business logic. Which attention points should the development team consider when implementing this solution?
optionA: Once that Apex runs on system mode, the development team needs to enforce record visibility.
optionB: Create test classes including runAs to test different users accessing the data.
optionC: Use isShareable, isEditable, and isCreatable to enforce field permissions.
explanation:
Once Apex runs in system mode, the development team needs to enforce record visibility — option A is the only choice that names a genuine security consideration, and it is the exam key.
The premise inside A has aged, so hold it precisely rather than as a slogan. Secure Apex Classes states that "In API version 66.0 and earlier, Apex runs in system mode by default", and that "In API version 67.0 and later, Apex runs in user mode by default, meaning that the current user's permissions and field-level security (FLS) are enforced during code execution." The same page adds that an @AuraEnabled class which sets neither with sharing nor without sharing "uses a default or implicit value of with sharing".
The durable lesson survives the version change: an LWC that reaches data through Apex does not inherit the UI's security for free, so declare the sharing keyword and the access mode explicitly on every class and query rather than relying on whichever default your API version happens to give you.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Create test classes including runAs) — good practice, but it describes a test, not an implementation concern for the view-and-logic split the stem asks about.
Option C (Use isShareable, isEditable, and isCreatable to enforce field permissions) — disqualified outright: "isShareable" does not exist, and the Schema describe methods are isAccessible, isCreateable and isUpdateable.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/lwc/guide/apex-security.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_enforce_usermode.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_perms_enforcing.htm
_cat: Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields

corrected.note: Answer stands, but "Apex runs in system mode" is version-dependent and is no longer the documented default: from API version 67.0 Apex runs in user mode by default, and an @AuraEnabled class with no sharing keyword already used an implicit "with sharing". Explanation rewritten so the option is not learned as a timeless rule.

question: If a Case requires involvement from one of the Legal team, the Case owner adds one of the corporate lawyers to the Legal SME field on the case. Since cases are private, how can we grant a lawyer access to a specific case when their assistance is needed?
optionA: Create a Criteria-Based Sharing Rule that shares to the Corporate Legal Team Role when the "legal assistance needed?" field is checked.
optionB: Use Apex Managed sharing in a case Trigger that shares the record to the user identified in the Legal SME field.
optionC: Create a Criteria Based Sharing Rule that shares to the Legal Public Group when the "legal assistance needed?" field is checked.
explanation:
Using Apex Managed sharing in a Case trigger that shares the record to the user identified in the Legal SME field is how the lawyer gets access. The lawyer is identified per record in the Legal SME user lookup, so the share target is dynamic, and only Apex managed sharing can share to whichever user populates that field on each case.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Criteria-Based Sharing Rule to the Corporate Legal Team Role) — a rule shares to a fixed role, so every lawyer in the role sees every flagged case, not the one lawyer named on it.
Option C (Criteria Based Sharing Rule to the Legal Public Group) — same limitation with a fixed public group; criteria-based rules cannot target an arbitrary user named in a field on each individual case.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) delivers training in 500 different regions. The UC operations users team manages course setup, scheduling, and trainer setup. The team members work at a regional level and report to an operations manager. The operations manager requested access to edit ALL scheduled courses owned by the operation users team. How should this be achieved?
optionA: The operations manager will get access to the scheduled courses by creating an ownership-based sharing rule and share the scheduled courses with the operations manager.
optionB: The operations manager will get access to the scheduled courses owned by the operations users team defined in the Role Hierarchy.
optionC: The operations manager will get access to the scheduled courses by creating a public group, and add the operations manager and the operations users team to the public group.
explanation:
The operations manager gets access to the scheduled courses owned by the operations users team through the Role Hierarchy. The manager sits above the regional operations users in the hierarchy, and the object grants access up the hierarchy by default, so the manager automatically gets edit access to all scheduled courses the team owns.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an ownership-based sharing rule to the operations manager) — unnecessary overhead: the hierarchy already grants a manager access to subordinates' records.
Option C (a public group containing the manager and the team) — a public group by itself confers no access; it is only a target for a sharing rule, and the ownership-based access requested is already provided by the hierarchy.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses Person Accounts to represent retail customers and Business Accounts to represent commercial customers. The retail sales team should not have access to commercial customers but should have access to ALL retail customers. With the organization-wide default on Account set to Private, how should the architect meet these requirements?
optionA: Create a criteria-based sharing rule giving the Retail Sales role access to Accounts of type Person Account.
optionB: Create an owner-based sharing rule on AccountContactRelation to grant access to all account contact roles records owned by retail sales reps.
optionC: Update the Retail Sales profile to grant access to Person Account record type.
explanation:
Creating a criteria-based sharing rule giving the Retail Sales role access to Accounts of type Person Account meets the requirement. With Account set to Private, a criteria-based rule matching the Person Account record type grants the Retail Sales role access to all retail customers while leaving Business (commercial) accounts hidden.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an owner-based sharing rule on AccountContactRelation) — shares contact-relationship records owned by retail reps; it grants no access to the Account records themselves, and misses retail accounts owned by anyone else.
Option C (Update the Retail Sales profile to grant access to the Person Account record type) — profile record-type access governs creation and layout assignment, not record visibility under a Private OWD.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a partner community for its 200 distributors. UC customer accounts are assigned an individual distributor. The organization-wide default setting for the custom Delivery object is Private. How should an architect advise UC to grant all users at a distributor access to delivery records for all customers assigned to a particular distributor?
optionA: Create a criteria based sharing rule that shares delivery records matching a distributor to the Distributor role in the Role Hierarchy.
optionB: Create a criteria-based sharing rule that shares delivery records matching the Distributor to users of a Public Group created for the distributor.
optionC: Create a Sharing Set for the Distributor profile to grant access to the Delivery object.
explanation:
Creating a Sharing Set for the Distributor profile to grant access to the Delivery object is the scalable answer for site users. A sharing set is configured per profile — "You can have one sharing set per profile only" — so a single Delivery mapping covers every user at every distributor instead of 200 per-distributor rules.
One caveat on the mapping. A sharing set grants access to records "associated with an account or contact that matches the user's account or contact", and access mappings support indirect lookups. Whether one mapping can reach Delivery records that hang off the customer account rather than the distributor account depends on how the Delivery-to-account relationship is modelled; if the lookup chain does not resolve to the user's own account, the sharing set has to be designed around that. Treat C as the right family of solution rather than a configuration you can copy unexamined.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (criteria-based sharing rule to the Distributor role in the Role Hierarchy) — partner users do have roles, but each partner account gets its own three-role hierarchy, so there is no single "Distributor role" to target; a rule per distributor does not scale to 200.
Option B (criteria-based sharing rule to a Public Group created for the distributor) — the same scaling problem: one public group and one rule per distributor, 200 of each, maintained by hand as distributors change.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers' organization wide-defaults model is Private for the Account object. A sales rep owns two opportunities in one Account. The Sales Rep profile has Create/Edit access to opportunity records. Which level of access will the sales rep have to the related Account record?
optionA: Read access
optionB: Read/Create/Edit access
optionC: No access
explanation:
Read access is the level the sales rep gets on the related Account. With the Account OWD Private, owning a child opportunity grants implicit Read-only access to the parent account so the related record is viewable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Read/Create/Edit access) — implicit parent sharing never grants edit or create on the parent; the profile's Create/Edit on Opportunity says nothing about Account.
Option C (No access) — implicit sharing from the child opportunity does grant read on the parent, so the rep is not locked out of the account.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_implicit_sharing.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has created a custom Invoice object. Standard sales users at UC can see the records in search layout, but when they click to view the detail, only record name, created date, and last modified date are shown. When the system admin accesses it, he or she sees the full record detail with many more data fields. What is the likely cause of this issue?
optionA: A role-based sharing rule is missing and should be added for the sales user's role to grant access to the fields.
optionB: The Sales Users profile does not have access to the remaining fields.
optionC: The page layout assigned to Sales User profile has only Read-Only access to the fields.
explanation:
The Sales Users profile not having access to the remaining fields is the likely cause. The user can open the record but sees only a few system fields while the admin sees everything, which is the signature of missing Field-Level Security on the profile; FLS is what determines which fields a profile can read.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a role-based sharing rule is missing) — sharing rules control record access, not field visibility; the users can already open the record.
Option C (the page layout has only Read-Only access to the fields) — a read-only layout would still display the fields rather than hide them.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.checking_field_accessibility_for_a_particular_field.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields

question: Universal Containers (UC) wants to reduce the amount of redundant leads entered into the system. UC also only edited/reassigned by the lead owner. What organization-wide default (OWD) approach should be recommended to help UC implement these requirements?
optionA: Implement a Public Read Only OWD on Lead.
optionB: Implement a Public Read Only/Transfer OWD on Lead
optionC: Implement a private OWD on Lead.
optionD: Implement a Public Read/Write OWD on Lead.
explanation:
Implementing a Public Read Only OWD on Lead satisfies both halves of the requirement. Reps can see every existing lead, which is what stops them entering a duplicate, while edit and reassignment stay with the owner and with users above the owner in the role hierarchy.
Note that "Public Read Only/Transfer" is not a real Lead setting; the transfer option Salesforce offers is Public Read/Write/Transfer.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Public Read Only/Transfer OWD on Lead) — not a setting that exists, and any transfer variant adds reassignment rights the requirement explicitly reserves for the owner.
Option C (a private OWD on Lead) — hides leads from everyone but their owner and defeats the deduplication goal outright.
Option D (Public Read/Write OWD on Lead) — hands editing to the whole org, contradicting "only edited/reassigned by the lead owner".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers would like to store an encryption key within Salesforce for use in Apex Code, but does not want users to be able to see this confidential key. Users require the view setup permission. How can Universal Containers securely store the confidential key?
optionA: Create a protected custom metadata type that stores the encryption key. Package the protected custom metadata type with its associated records in a managed package. Install the package in the production org.
optionB: Create a protected custom metadata type that stores the encryption key. Package the protected custom metadata type with its associated records in an unlocked package. Install the package in the production org.
optionC: Create a custom metadata type that stores the encryption key. Make sure that only the admin profile has access to the custom metadata type so that end users cannot access the encryption key.
explanation:
Creating a protected custom metadata type, packaging it with its records in a managed package and installing that package in production is how the key stays confidential. A protected custom metadata type packaged in a managed package hides its records even from users who hold View Setup, so the encryption key stays invisible while remaining usable in Apex.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (protected custom metadata type in an unlocked package) — an unlocked package does not protect the records the way a managed package does; protected visibility depends on the managed namespace.
Option C (custom metadata type restricted to the admin profile) — plain custom metadata in the subscriber org is viewable through Setup by anyone with View Setup, and there is no profile-level access control on custom metadata records.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.custommetadatatypes_package_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a fast-growing company that sells containers globally. It has thousands of dealerships throughout the world where local dealers service containers. UC implemented a new Partner Community for its dealers. Each dealership has a dealer manager who manages the service agents. The community sharing model is private. What is the optimal option to give dealer managers visibility to customer cases only raised by their service agents?
optionA: Use the Role Hierarchy so that the cases raised by service agents will be visible to their relevant dealer managers.
optionB: Create a sharing rule to share cases created by service agents with their dealer manager.
optionC: Create a sharing group to share cases created by service agents with their dealer manager.
explanation:
Using the Role Hierarchy so that cases raised by service agents are visible to their relevant dealer managers is the optimal option. In a private community model, dealer managers sit above their service agents in the partner Role Hierarchy, so cases owned by the agents roll up to their manager automatically with no extra configuration.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a sharing rule to share cases with their dealer manager) — unnecessary: the hierarchy already provides this, and one rule per dealership does not scale to thousands.
Option C (a sharing group) — not a construct for this hierarchy-based visibility; groups are only targets for rules and would again need one per dealership.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The finance team at Universal Containers usually does not have access to account and contact records. A finance analyst was temporarily given opportunity access for a big deal to help with tax calculation. However, she can now also access account and contact records. What is causing this issue?
optionA: Account records can be accessed due to implicit sharing from Opportunity.
optionB: Account records can be accessed due to Role Hierarchy.
optionC: Contact records can be accessed due to implicit sharing from Opportunity.
explanation:
Account records being accessible due to implicit sharing from Opportunity is what is causing this. Granting access to an opportunity gives implicit Read access to its parent account and related contacts, which is why the finance analyst can suddenly see the account; this is by-design implicit parent sharing from the opportunity.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Account records can be accessed due to Role Hierarchy) — the analyst's role did not change; the cause is the opportunity access she was just given.
Option C (Contact records can be accessed due to implicit sharing from Opportunity) — the question concerns the account specifically, and the documented implicit grant from an opportunity is to its parent account; contact visibility here follows from the account.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_implicit_sharing.htm

question: Universal Containers has implemented Customer Community with Customer Community Plus licenses for its distributors. Some distributors requested granting specific community users (agents) to view cases submitted by other agents of the same distributor. Which feature only supports these requirements?
optionA: Permission set to grant community admin permission
optionB: Delegate external user
optionC: Partner super user
explanation:
Partner super user is the feature that supports this. Customer Community Plus has roles, and the Partner/Customer Super User permission lets a user see records owned by other users of the same account at their role and below, which is exactly "view cases of other agents of the same distributor."
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Permission set to grant community admin permission) — manages users and the community; it does not grant visibility into records owned by other agents.
Option B (Delegate external user) — delegated external user administration lets a user create and manage other external users; it is user administration, not record visibility.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_super_user_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Who can view a PDF that is uploaded to the Files Home private library by a user?
optionA: The user and users above them in the Role Hierarchy
optionB: The user and users with View All Data permission
optionC: Only the user
explanation:
Only the user can view a PDF uploaded to a Files Home private library. Who Can See My File? makes the point twice over, once for each of the permissions people expect to override it: "Users with Modify All Data permission have built-in access to files that they don't own… However, if the file is in a private library, then only the file owner has access to it", and "Users with View All Data permission can view and preview files that they don't own. However, if the file is in a private library, then only the file owner has access to it."
One distinction the stem blurs: a plain upload in Files home is private in the sense that it has not been shared, but the owner plus users with Modify All Data can still find it. Only the private library carves out even those permissions.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The user and users above them in the Role Hierarchy) — the role hierarchy does not enter into it at all; file visibility is not derived from role.
Option B (The user and users with View All Data permission) — View All Data normally reaches unowned files, but the documentation carves out the private library explicitly: only the owner has access there.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.collab_files_settings_perms.htm&type=5

question: Besides their own team accounts, sales managers at Universal Containers (UC) need Read access to all accounts of the same segment in other countries. Role Hierarchy was implemented accordingly (based on countries), but a sales manager in the U.S. is complaining that he cannot view account records of the same segment in Canada. What should UC do to grant access properly?
optionA: Create an owner-based sharing rule to grant access to account records, that have the same segment, to all sales manager roles.
optionB: Create a public group and include all accounts of the same segment, and then grant access with a permission set.
optionC: Change the Role Hierarchy and put all the sales managers in the U.S. and Canada in the same role.
explanation:
Creating an owner-based sharing rule that grants all sales manager roles access to account records with the same segment is what UC should do. A sharing rule that shares same-segment accounts to every sales-manager role gives the U.S. manager visibility into Canadian same-segment accounts that the country-based Role Hierarchy cannot provide laterally. Note the option says "owner-based," though sharing on a segment value is technically criteria-based, so the wording is imprecise.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a public group of accounts plus a permission set) — public groups contain users, not accounts, and a permission set cannot grant record access based on a segment value.
Option C (put all U.S. and Canadian sales managers in the same role) — merging the roles would break the country hierarchy the org deliberately built.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US

question: Dreamforce presenters need to be able to edit their presentation details (summary, presenter biographies, etc) on a private custom object in Salesforce (Presentation). All presenters for a presentation are captured on a Presenters junction object between Presenter and User. How can this be accomplished?
optionA: Give Edit rights to the Presentation record via a Permission set that is given to the Presenters for a record.
optionB: Trigger on Presenter junction object that adds the user to the Sales Team for the Presentation record.
optionC: Trigger on Presenter junction object that uses Apex Managed sharing to add or remove access to the related Presentation record.
explanation:
A trigger on the Presenter junction object that uses Apex Managed sharing to add or remove access to the related Presentation record is how this is accomplished. Presenters are linked through a junction and need edit access on the related private Presentation, so a trigger that maintains share rows as junction records are created and deleted is the precise solution.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Edit rights via a Permission set given to the Presenters) — a permission set grants object-level access to every Presentation record, not record-level access to one presentation.
Option B (Trigger that adds the user to the Sales Team) — sales teams (account and opportunity teams) exist only for those standard objects; there is no team on a custom Presentation object.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has affiliates who sell containers in countries where UC does not have a local office. UC uses a Partner Community to manage the sales cycle in those countries. One of its affiliates has grown substantially and restructured its internal sales team with the following structure: Sales VP -> Director of Sales -> Sales Manager -> Sales Reps. Sales Reps should not see each others' opportunities, and visibility of deals should open up within a Sales Rep's hierarchy. What is the main problem an architect should address in this situation?
optionA: The Channel Manager role cannot be shared with Partner Community.
optionB: Partner User roles are limited to three Ievels.
optionC: Partner Community does not support Role Hierarchy.
explanation:
Partner User roles being limited to three levels is the main problem to address. Partner Community provides only three partner role levels, so a four-tier reseller hierarchy of VP, Director, Manager, and Rep cannot be modeled directly; the limitation is the depth, not the existence, of partner roles.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The Channel Manager role cannot be shared with Partner Community) — the channel manager is an internal role above the partner account's roles; nothing in the scenario needs it shared, and it is not what blocks a four-level partner structure.
Option C (Partner Community does not support Role Hierarchy) — false: partner users do get a role hierarchy, up to three levels per partner account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers uses the standard Case object to track various support requests sent to servicing agents. Currently, the Case object has more than 400 fields. Eight different types of case processes have been established, each with a unique combination of statuses. The Director of Customer Service wants to ensure that servicing agents see only the required information specific to the case type they are addressing. Which option is recommended to implement this requirement?
optionA: Use Dynamic Forms with different field sections representing the relevant fields per case type, and control visibility of sections by Case Record Type value.
optionB: Use different Page Layouts per case type, each representing the relevant fields per case type.
optionC: Use a custom LWC to override the View action of the Case object, and a Custom Metadata Type to define the relevant fields per case type.
explanation:
Using Dynamic Forms with field sections per case type, with section visibility controlled by the Case Record Type value, is the recommended option. Dynamic Forms lets you place fields in sections and show or hide them by record type on a single Lightning page, meeting the requirement to show only the relevant fields per case type with minimal layouts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (different Page Layouts per case type) — the classic alternative and defensible, but eight layouts over 400 fields are heavier to maintain than one page with visibility rules.
Option C (custom LWC override of the View action plus a Custom Metadata Type) — adds unnecessary code for something the platform does declaratively.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.dynamic_forms_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.checking_field_accessibility_for_a_particular_field.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A custom Invoice object has been created with a master-detail relationship to Account. The accounts receivable (AR) team needs access to invoice records. AR users neither own nor have access to account records. The Account organization-wide default is set to Private. The AR team is unable to find invoices in list views, reports, and Global Search. The architect has been asked to help troubleshoot. What is preventing AR team members from seeing invoices?
optionA: The AR profile does not have Read permission to the Invoice object.
optionB: A sharing rule is missing to share invoices with the AR team.
optionC: A sharing rule is missing to share accounts with the AR team.
explanation:
A sharing rule being missing to share accounts with the AR team is what is preventing them from seeing invoices. Because Invoice is master-detail to Account, invoice access is Controlled by Parent, so the AR team cannot see invoices because they cannot see the parent accounts; sharing the Accounts with AR restores visibility everywhere, including list views, reports, and Global Search.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The AR profile does not have Read permission to the Invoice object) — the team already has object Read; the stem's symptoms are record-level, not object-level.
Option B (A sharing rule is missing to share invoices with the AR team) — a detail record in a master-detail relationship cannot be shared directly; its access is inherited from the master.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_manytomany.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has expanded to sell virtual containers for data storage. Virtual container work orders are provisioned immediately by the system and therefore cannot be changed by a sales rep. What is an optimal approach to implement these requirements?
optionA: Change the Record Type/Page Layout assignment for Work Orders to Read Only.
optionB: Implement a sharing rule that changes access for all Work Orders to Read.
optionC: Remove the Work Order Edit permission from the Sales Representative profile.
explanation:
Removing the Work Order Edit permission from the Sales Representative profile is the optimal approach. Provisioned virtual work orders must be non-editable by reps, and removing the Edit object permission is the clean, system-wide enforcement that holds in the UI, the API and Apex alike.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Change the Record Type/Page Layout assignment to Read Only) — a read-only layout does not block edits made through the API, list views or other layouts.
Option B (a sharing rule that changes access for all Work Orders to Read) — sharing rules only open access wider than the OWD; they cannot reduce an owner's or a profile's edit capability.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5
_cat: Permissions to Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and Fields

question: Users at Universal Containers are complaining that a field has disappeared from the Account page after last weekend's deployment. The page layout did not change with this deployment. How should the admin troubleshoot this issue?
optionA: View Field Accessibility in the Object Manager.
optionB: Log in as a user and check several accounts to isolate the problem records.
optionC: Run a Who Sees What report, filtering on Account.
explanation:
Viewing Field Accessibility in the Object Manager is how the admin should troubleshoot. A field disappearing without a layout change points to a Field-Level Security or accessibility change, and the Field Accessibility viewer shows per profile and record type whether a field is hidden or read-only, pinpointing the cause quickly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Log in as a user and check several accounts) — slower and less targeted; the field is missing for a whole population, not on particular records.
Option C (Run a Who Sees What report, filtering on Account) — that tooling is about record-level visibility, not whether one field is hidden by FLS.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.checking_field_accessibility_for_a_particular_field.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An architect has a requirement to create a criteria-based sharing rule based on the customer Social Security Number. However, when setting up the rule in Contact Sharing, the field is not shown on the list of available fields. What is causing this issue?
optionA: The architect does not have permission to Compliance fields.
optionB: The field has been configured for encryption.
optionC: The architect's profile does not have Field-Level Security for this field.
explanation:
The field having been configured for encryption is what is causing this. Classic-encrypted fields cannot be used in criteria-based sharing rule filters, so the encrypted Social Security Number field is absent from the available-fields list; that is the platform restriction at play.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The architect does not have permission to Compliance fields) — there is no "Compliance fields" permission that hides a field from the sharing-rule picker.
Option C (The architect's profile does not have Field-Level Security for this field) — lacking FLS would hide the field on layouts but is not why it is specifically unavailable for sharing-rule criteria.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.fields_about_encrypted_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which option can be selected to share data when creating a sharing rule?
optionA: Roles
optionB: users
optionC: Profiles
explanation:
Roles is the option that can be selected. When creating a sharing rule, the "share with" target can be public groups, roles, or roles and subordinates, so among these options Roles is the valid choice.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (users) — a sharing rule cannot share directly to individual users; put them in a public group first.
Option C (Profiles) — profiles are not a sharing-rule target; they govern object and field permissions, not record sharing.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a non-profit organization with more than 20,000,000 members (donors). UC decided to assign those accounts to donations reps based on their regions. Donations reps ended up owning more than 50,000 donors each. The donation reps started to see significant degradation of the system performance. What is the reason for this problem?
optionA: The donations reps' access to the assigned accounts is wrong.
optionB: Salesforce sharing recalculation kicked off.
optionC: There is an Account ownership data skew problem.
explanation:
An Account ownership data skew problem is the reason. Tens of thousands of accounts owned by individual donation reps creates ownership skew, which causes sharing and recalculation contention and the observed performance degradation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The donations reps' access to the assigned accounts is wrong) — the access design itself is not wrong; owners are meant to see their accounts.
Option B (Salesforce sharing recalculation kicked off) — recalculation is a symptom of the skew, not the root cause; it hurts because each rep owns 50,000 records.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm

question: A sales rep at Universal Containers was added to an opportunity team with Read/Write permissions. Which action is she allowed to perform in the opportunity?
optionA: Replace opportunity owner.
optionB: Update opportunity stage.
optionC: Add/remove members in the opportunity team.
explanation:
Updating the opportunity stage is the action she is allowed to perform. An Opportunity Team member with Read/Write can edit the record's fields, such as the stage.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Replace opportunity owner) — transferring ownership is reserved for the owner, users above the owner in the hierarchy, and users with Transfer permissions; team Read/Write does not include it.
Option C (Add/remove members in the opportunity team) — managing the team is an owner-only action; a Read/Write member cannot change its membership.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.salesteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales rep (John) at Universal Containers (UC) requested to update information in an account record where he has READ only access. John requested the EDIT access permission from the owner of the record (Paul). Paul manually shared the record with John. Assuming the OWD of the Account object is Public Read-Only, what is the impact in the system?
optionA: New AccountShare record is created. Row Cause is "Manual" and Access Level is "Read/Write".
optionB: Existing AccountShare record is updated. Row Cause is "Owner" and User/Group is "John".
optionC: New AccountShare record is created. Row Cause is "Owner" and Access Level is "Full".
optionD: Existing AccountShare record is updated. Row Cause is "Manual" and Access Level is "Read/Write".
explanation:
A new AccountShare record is created with Row Cause "Manual" and Access Level "Read/Write". Manually granting Read/Write on a Public Read-Only account creates a new share row with row cause Manual; the baseline Read-only access comes from the OWD rather than from an "Owner" share row that gets updated.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Existing AccountShare updated, Row Cause "Owner", User/Group "John") — the Owner row belongs to Paul and is never rewritten to another user; a manual share is a separate row.
Option C (New AccountShare, Row Cause "Owner", Access Level "Full") — Owner rows are created only for the record owner; a manual share carries the Manual row cause and the access level granted, not Full.
Option D (Existing AccountShare updated, Row Cause "Manual", Access Level "Read/Write") — there was no existing Manual row for John to update; John's read access came from the OWD, which has no share row at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.granting_access_to_records_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales Operations at Universal Containers (UC) has created Public Report and Dashboard folders for sales managers that report to the VP of sales. Sales Operations currently spends a few hours each month updating users that should have access to edit items in these folders. In which two ways can UC grant access to sales managers to automate access to these Reports and Dashboards folders? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Share the folders lowest roles in the role hierarchy, Superiors will get access automatically.
optionB: Share the folders with the "VP of Sales" Role and Subordinates.
optionC: Share the folders with the "Sales Managers" Queue.
optionD: Share the folders with a "Sales Managers" Public Group.
explanation:
Sharing the folders with the "VP of Sales" Role and Subordinates, and sharing them with a "Sales Managers" Public Group, are the two ways. Report and dashboard folders can be shared with a role and its subordinates or with a public group, both of which automatically include the right managers and eliminate the monthly manual upkeep.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Share the folders with the lowest roles; superiors get access automatically) — folder access does not roll up the role hierarchy, so superiors would not inherit it.
Option C (Share the folders with the "Sales Managers" Queue) — folders cannot be shared with queues; the targets are users, public groups and roles.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.access_report_folders.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.analytics_sharing_permissions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales reps at Universal Containers (UC) complain about the manual activities they need to perform in order to grant access to supporting internal users (legal, engineering, finance, etc.) for customer records when they need help. In general, the sales reps involved in the deals will not change. How should an architect help UC improve sales reps' productivity?
optionA: Create a permission set with View All Data and assign to supporting users.
optionB: Create a criteria based sharing rule to grant access to other users.
optionC: Leverage default Account team.
explanation:
Leveraging the default Account team is how the architect should improve productivity. Because the same supporting users repeatedly help on the rep's deals, a default Account Team auto-adds them to new accounts, removing the manual sharing while scoping access appropriately.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a permission set with View All Data) — massively over-grants; every supporting user would see every record in the org.
Option B (a criteria based sharing rule) — a rule cannot express "the specific helpers this particular rep works with"; the pattern is per rep, not per record criteria.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: An architect from a previous project implemented Platform Shield Encryption for a company. However, based on a recent audit, the company's Privacy Team identified three additional fields in their Account Records (Billing Street, Billing City and Phone) that needs to be secure and protected. How should an architect proceed with this new policy change?
optionA: Use Encryption Policy and contact Salesforce to update the existing records so that their field values are encrypted.
optionB: Use Encryption Policy and wait for an email from Salesforce indicating the field values are encrypted.
optionC: Use Classic Encryption to ensure all fields are protected and contact Salesforce for help with encryption verification.
explanation:
Using the Encryption Policy and contacting Salesforce to update the existing records so that their field values are encrypted is how to proceed. Turning on encryption for Billing Street, Billing City and Phone through the encryption policy protects data written from that point on; values already stored stay in the clear until they are re-saved or run through background encryption. So the policy change is only half the job, and the second half is a synchronisation step.
How that step is triggered has changed since this item was written. Salesforce now supports self-service synchronisation from the Encryption Statistics and Data Sync page in Setup for standard and custom fields, the Attachment Content Body field, and field history and feed tracking — with a limit of once every seven days. For everything outside that list you still contact Salesforce Customer Support. Option A therefore remains correct in substance: an explicit background-encryption pass is required, and Salesforce may still have to run it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Use Encryption Policy and wait for an email from Salesforce) — nothing happens to existing values on its own; no email arrives because no background pass has been requested.
Option C (Use Classic Encryption and contact Salesforce for verification) — Classic Encryption is a separate and weaker feature that applies only to custom text fields, so it cannot protect standard Account fields.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.security_pe_mass_encryption.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: (Variant) Which method should be used to grant an unrelated group of users access to a set of records?
optionA: Role Hierarchy
optionB: Sharing Sets
optionC: Public Groups
explanation:
Public Groups are the method to use. A public group is what you build when the people who need access do not line up with anything the platform already models. Salesforce describes exactly this use: "Use public groups to streamline sharing records with users in different parts of your company that aren't aligned with a single role." Collect the users in the group, then point a sharing rule at it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Role Hierarchy) — models reporting lines, so it cannot express an arbitrary, unrelated set of users.
Option B (Sharing Sets) — grant site users access to records tied to their own account or contact; a community mechanism, not a way to hand a group of internal users a set of records.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What advanced tool can Salesforce enable for Large-scale role hierarchy realignments?
optionA: Set external organization-wide default to public read only
optionB: Skinny Table Indexing
optionC: Granular locking
optionD: Partitioning by Divisions
explanation:
Granular locking is the advanced tool that makes large realignments survivable. Without it, the sharing system takes a lock over the whole group-membership table during updates, so unrelated role and group changes queue behind one another and callers see "could not acquire lock" errors. With it, "groups that are in separate hierarchies can be manipulated concurrently", users can be added to territories and public groups at the same time, and "a single long-running process, such as a role delete, blocks only a small subset of operations".
Worth knowing for current orgs: granular locking is now enabled by default, so this is less a switch you ask Salesforce to flip than a behaviour you design your maintenance processes around. Salesforce publishes a table of which group operations may run concurrently.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Set external organization-wide default to public read only) — an external OWD governs what site users can see; it has nothing to do with recalculation locking.
Option B (Skinny Table Indexing) — skinny tables improve query and report performance; they do not touch group-membership locks.
Option D (Partitioning by Divisions) — Divisions partition data for searches and reports, not the sharing recalculation a hierarchy realignment triggers.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: Sales operations at Universal Containers (UC) wants to create list views to filter opportunities for certain geographies. How should UC hide list views that are not relevant to an individual user since there will be more than 50 list views?
optionA: Share the list views with the appropriate public group.
optionB: Share the list views with the appropriate queue.
optionC: Share the list views with the appropriate individual users.
explanation:
Sharing the list views with the appropriate public group is how UC should hide irrelevant views. List views are made visible to a chosen set of users by sharing them with a public group, so each geography's reps see only the views relevant to them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Share the list views with the appropriate queue) — list views can be shared with public groups or roles, not with queues.
Option C (Share the list views with the appropriate individual users) — per-user sharing does not scale across more than fifty views and every staffing change.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387584&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: To grant Universal Containers sales managers access to shipment records properly, it was necessary to leverage Apex managed sharing. The IT team is worried about improper access to records. What should an architect recommend to mitigate this risk?
optionA: Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility will be followed.
optionB: Use isAccessible keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility will be followed.
optionC: Use runAs system method in test classes to test using different users and profiles.
explanation:
Using the runAs system method in test classes to test with different users and profiles is what the architect should recommend. Apex managed sharing is created by code running in system context, so the safeguard available here is proof by testing: runAs lets a test assume each affected user and assert what that user can actually see. Using the runAs Method states that inside the block "the user's sharing rules and object-level and field-level permissions are enforced... regardless of the sharing mode (with sharing or without sharing) of the test class".
Note what this option set omits: declaring the class with sharing, which is the construct that actually re-imposes record visibility on the code. With that absent, runAs is the only genuine safeguard on the list.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes) — isShareable is not a member of Apex's Schema.DescribeSObjectResult at all; it is not a construct.
Option B (Use isAccessible keyword in Apex classes) — isAccessible() does exist and returns "true if the current user can see this object", but it is a describe method for object-level access rather than a keyword, and it reports nothing about individual record visibility.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_runas.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_sobject_describe.htm

question: Universal Containers has selected a small and diverse group of users to review Inactive accounts. Given the Private sharing model, a public group was created and made available to this group of users. A sharing rule was created to make inactive Accounts visible to the public group. However, some of these users are reporting they don't see any of the Accounts that were shared with the public group. what is the underlying Issue for these users?
optionA: The users are in profiles that have no access to the Account object.
optionB: The page layout assigned to these users is different than the Account owner.
optionC: The users have a permission set that only allow Accounts in "Active' status.
optionD: The Accounts are owned by users higher in the role hierarchy.
explanation:
The users being in profiles that have no access to the Account object is the underlying issue. Sharing rules extend record access only on top of object-level CRUD, so users whose profiles lack Read on Account see nothing regardless of the sharing rule; object access is the prerequisite the affected users are missing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a different page layout than the Account owner) — a layout changes how a record displays, not whether it is visible at all.
Option C (a permission set that only allows Accounts in "Active" status) — permission sets grant object and field permissions; they cannot filter records by a status value.
Option D (The Accounts are owned by users higher in the role hierarchy) — the sharing rule to the public group grants access regardless of the owner's position; owner rank would not blank out every shared account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5
