question: A user posts a file to the Chatter feed for a record of an object that has a Private organization-wide default. Which statement accurately describes who can view the file by default?
optionA: Only the user who posted the file
optionB: The user who posted the file and users with access to the record
optionC: The user who posted the file and users with a shared chatter post link to the file
explanation:
The user who posted the file and users with access to the record can view it. A file posted to a record's Chatter feed inherits that record's sharing, so it is visible to the poster and to anyone who has access to the private record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Only the user who posted the file) — the file is attached to the record's feed, so everyone who can see the record can see it; it is not private to the poster.
Option C (The poster and users with a shared chatter post link) — visibility follows record access by default, not a link; a user with the link but no record access still cannot open it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.collab_files_settings_perms.htm&type=5

question: Which community function is impacted by having the Site User Visibility turned off in Sharing Settings?
optionA: Searching for other external users.
optionB: Updating their user profile.
optionC: Searching for internal users.
explanation:
Searching for other external users is the function impacted. Disabling Site (community) User Visibility stops community users from finding other external users in search.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Updating their user profile) — a user's ability to edit their own profile is unaffected by whether they can see other users.
Option C (Searching for internal users) — internal user visibility to site users is governed separately; Site User Visibility concerns external-to-external visibility.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_user_sharing.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
The sales managers at Universal Containers requested their teams to define each user's role on their accounts in order to provide an easy way to establish accountability and collaboration. Sales managers also requested that sales associates should only get the following permissions:
1. Read access to the accounts.
2. Read access to cases related to the accounts.
3. No access to deals related to the accounts.
The sales associates may be granted access to opportunities when needed. Assuming the overall sharing model of the organization is Private and no sharing rules are configured on the Account object, how should an architect achieve these requirements?
optionA: Use Account teams to define access to accounts as well as opportunities and cases related to accounts.
optionB: Use Account teams and Case teams. No configuration required for the Opportunity object.
optionC: Use Account teams and sharing rules to share cases with sales associates. No change required to the Opportunity object.
explanation:
Using Account teams to define access to accounts as well as the opportunities and cases related to them is how the architect achieves this. A single Account Team can grant the defined per-user access, namely Read on accounts and related cases and no opportunity access unless explicitly granted, covering all three requirements through one mechanism.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Account teams and Case teams, no Opportunity configuration) — unnecessary: Account Team membership already carries a case access level, so Case teams add a second mechanism for the same grant.
Option C (Account teams and sharing rules for cases, no Opportunity change) — also unnecessary, and a sharing rule shares cases to a role or group rather than to the specific associates on each account.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Customer complaints for bad interactions with a customer support agent are logged as Cases and assigned to a human resources representative. The agent of the complaint should not see the case, but their manager should. How is this accomplished?
optionA: Trigger on Case to lookup and share to the manager of an Assigned Agent custom field (the subject of the complaint) using Apex Managed Sharing.
optionB: Criteria based Sharing Rule on Case that shares to the Role Manager and above when a custom field Assigned Agent (subject of the complaint) Is not blank,
optionC: Case is owned by the subject of the complaint, so their manager in the role hierarchy can access the record. CRED permission are removed on Case so the agent cannot read the case record.
explanation:
A trigger on Case that looks up the manager of the Assigned Agent custom field and shares to that manager using Apex Managed Sharing is how this is accomplished. The complaint must be hidden from the agent but visible to their manager, identified per record through a custom field, so a dynamic share to that manager is the precise solution.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Criteria based Sharing Rule to the Role Manager and above) — over-shares up the whole chain and cannot target the one manager of the agent named on each case.
Option C (Case owned by the subject of the complaint, CRED removed) — owning the case would let the agent see it, and removing CRED on Case would also stop the manager and HR reading any case.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers has created a Reimbursement Custom Object to capture requests for reimbursement of expenses related to office supplies. The Reimbursement requests are sometimes sensitive and the Team Leads should not have access to the Reimbursement records submitted by the Users in the Call Center Agent role. The Director of Support will require access to all Reimbursement records. The role hierarchy is set as follows: Call Center Agent role reports to Team Lead role, which Reports to the Director of Support. Which steps would the Architect take to ensure proper sharing in this Role Hierarchy structure assuming Private Sharing Setting for the Reimbursement Object?
optionA: Leave the Reimbursement Object in "Deployed" Status and set the Director of Supports Profile to "View All" in the object permissions.
optionB: Use an Approval Process to change the owner of the Reimbursement record upon submission to the Director of Support
optionC: Disable Grant Access Using Hierarchies for the Object and create a Sharing Rule to enable sharing to the Director of Support
optionD: The sharing scenario described will occur without any special configuration choices being made by the Architect
explanation:
Disabling Grant Access Using Hierarchies for the object and creating a Sharing Rule to the Director of Support are the steps. Because the Director sits above the Team Leads, hiding reimbursements from Team Leads while still giving the Director access means you must switch off hierarchy inheritance on the custom object, then add a sharing rule granting the Director access.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Leave the object Deployed and set View All on the Director's profile) — View All gives the Director access but does nothing to stop Team Leads inheriting subordinate records through the hierarchy.
Option B (an Approval Process that changes the owner to the Director on submission) — a workaround that misuses ownership as a sharing mechanism: the agent loses access to their own request, the Director must own every record, and nothing is configured for the object's actual sharing.
Option D (no special configuration needed) — the default behavior exposes the records to Team Leads through Grant Access Using Hierarchies.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US

question: Universal Containers has a global 24x7 Salesforce.com implementation that supports Sales, Services, Order Management, and various other parts of their business. They have a nested territory hierarchy, 10,000 sales users, and 20,000 support agents. Territory changes happen daily. The demand for new applications and changes to the platform is high and they follow an agile development methodology and deliver new releases every two weeks on the platform. What Salesforce.com feature would help the system recover from a maintenance restart on Salesforce.com servers?
optionA: Enable Granular Locking on the system.
optionB: Enable Deferred Sharing Rule recalculation.
optionC: Enable Parallel Sharing Rule recalculation.
optionD: Enable Filter-Based Opportunity Territory Assignment.
explanation:
Enabling Parallel Sharing Rule recalculation is what helps the system recover from a maintenance restart — recovery is what parallel recalculation buys you, not deferral. Salesforce describes asynchronous parallel recalculation of sharing rules as running "in parallel and asynchronously in the background, which speeds up the process and provides better resilience to site operations such as patches and server restarts" — that resilience is the documented answer to this scenario.
Deferred sharing calculations solve a different problem. They are a planned-maintenance tool: an admin suspends group-membership and sharing-rule processing, makes a batch of role, group and rule changes inside a negotiated window, then resumes and manually kicks off a full recalculation. Nothing about deferral helps an org absorb an unplanned restart — and if calculations are still suspended when one happens, access rights are simply stale until someone resumes them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Enable Granular Locking) — addresses concurrency between group-maintenance operations, not recovery of an interrupted recalculation.
Option B (Enable Deferred Sharing Rule recalculation) — a planned-maintenance-window tool that suspends calculation and needs a manual full recalculation afterwards; it offers no resilience to an unplanned restart.
Option D (Enable Filter-Based Opportunity Territory Assignment) — an unrelated Sales feature for routing opportunities to territories.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_recalculating_parallel.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_defer_sharing_calculations.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_tools_deferred_sharing_maintenance.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved from Deferred Sharing Rule recalculation to Parallel Sharing Rule Recalculation. Salesforce documents parallel recalculation as providing "better resilience to site operations such as patches and server restarts"; deferral is a planned-maintenance-window tool that suspends calculation and requires a manual full recalculation afterwards. (The resilience wording is carried in the Security Implementation Guide through v240; the current help article describes the same asynchronous parallel behaviour.)

question: Universal Containers has a strict security model enforced through object, field, and row-based security mechanisms. The Architect would like to ensure the security model is being thoroughly tested using Apex automated tests. Which three considerations should be made when using the runAs() method to design Apex until tests?
optionA: runAs() does not enforce user permissions or field-level permissions in test classes
optionB: runAs() can be used inside of test classes to validate record-level security
optionC: runAs() can be used inside of test classes to validate field-level permissions
optionD: runAs() can be used outside of test classes to bypass record-level security
optionE: runAs () counts towards total DML statements issued within transaction
explanation:
runAs() not enforcing user or field-level permissions in test classes, runAs() validating record-level security inside test classes, and runAs() counting towards DML statements are the three keyed considerations, and two of them are solid. runAs can only be used inside a test method, and it is the way a test validates record-level security (B); and "Every call to runAs counts against the total number of DML statements issued in the process" (E).
Option A is the legacy statement and no longer matches the documentation. Using the runAs Method now says that inside a runAs block "the user's sharing rules and object-level and field-level permissions are enforced", regardless of the test class's sharing mode. On that reading option C — validating field-level permissions — is also true, which makes this a choose-three with four defensible options.
Keep A as the exam key, but know why it is contested: outside runAs, Apex generally runs in system mode and ignores the running user's object and field permissions, which is the fact the option is reaching for. Inside the block, the documentation says those permissions apply.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (runAs() can validate field-level permissions) — true under the current documentation, but it contradicts the keyed option A and is not what the exam keys; the item is defective as printed.
Option D (runAs() can be used outside of test classes to bypass record-level security) — false for the same reason B is true: runAs is test-only and cannot be called from production code.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_runas.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_perms_enforcing.htm

corrected.note: Key stands, but option A ("runAs does not enforce user permissions or field-level permissions") contradicts the current Apex Developer Guide, which states that object-level and field-level permissions are enforced within a runAs block. That also makes option C arguably true, so the choose-three has four defensible options. Flagged as defective rather than re-keyed, because A is the answer the exam tests.

question: An External Object is created to show Invoices from an external accounting system. When viewing the External Object, a user should only access invoice records the user is authorized to see. What two actions are required to achieve the above requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Setup External Object to use OAuth to connect to the Accounting system.
optionB: Create an owner based sharing rule to grant visibility to the Invoice object.
optionC: Restrict access to data in the accounting system.
optionD: Grant access to the External Object to only the Account Manager profile.
explanation:
Setting up the External Object to use OAuth to connect to the Accounting system, and restricting access to data in the accounting system, are the two required actions. External Object rows live in the external system, so per-user authorization is enforced there: connect via OAuth so each user authenticates as themselves, and restrict the data in the accounting system itself.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (an owner based sharing rule on the Invoice object) — Salesforce sharing rules do not filter external-object rows; the rows are not owned or stored in Salesforce.
Option D (Grant access to the External Object only to the Account Manager profile) — a profile grant is object-level; it cannot restrict which invoice rows a given user sees.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.salesforce_connect_odata.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which three capabilities are available with Enterprise Territory Management? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Create a public group with Territory
optionB: Share a report or dashboard folder with a Territory
optionC: Metadata API Support
optionD: Integration with Collaborative Forecasting
explanation:
Metadata API Support, Integration with Collaborative Forecasting, and Assignment of Territory on Opportunities are the three keyed capabilities, and all three are real Enterprise Territory Management capabilities. Salesforce's own comparison of original Territory Management and ETM lists Metadata API Support as No for the original feature and Yes for ETM, Integration with Collaborative Forecasts as No and Yes, and Assignment of Territory on Opportunities as Yes for both (available in ETM since Spring '15).
The item is defective, though, because the same table marks the other two options Yes for ETM as well: "Share a Report / Dashboard Folder with a Territory — Yes" and "Create a Public Group with Territory — Yes". Five options, five true statements, three answer slots.
If you want the discriminators that actually separate the two generations, they are the ones the table marks No for original Territory Management: territory models, territory types and priority, multiple hierarchies, audit trail, Metadata API support, Collaborative Forecasts integration, and rule sharing among territories.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Create a public group with Territory) — not wrong in fact: the comparison table marks it Yes for ETM. It is excluded only because the exam keys the three capabilities that distinguish ETM from the original feature.
Option B (Share a report or dashboard folder with a Territory) — likewise available in ETM per the same table; excluded for the same reason, and the item cannot be answered from the documentation alone.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387747&language=en_US&type=1

corrected.note: Answers stand, but the old explanation asserted that you cannot create a public group with a territory or share a report/dashboard folder with a territory. Salesforce's Territory Management comparison table marks both as available in Enterprise Territory Management, so all five options are true and the choose-three cannot be answered as printed.

question: Universal Containers has set up Partner users, who will see records owned by partner users in roles below them in the hierarchy. Which three roles make up the partner role hierarchy?
optionA: Owner, Manager, and User
optionB: Executive, Manager, and Worker
optionC: Executive, Manager, and User
optionD: Administrator, Manager, and User
explanation:
Executive, Manager, and User are the three roles. Enabling a partner account creates a three-tier role hierarchy beneath that account — Partner Executive, Partner Manager, and Partner User. A partner user sees records owned by partner users at the roles below their own within that account, so an Executive sees Manager- and User-owned records, a Manager sees User-owned records, and a User sees only their own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Owner, Manager, and User) — there is no "Owner" partner role; the top tier is Executive.
Option B (Executive, Manager, and Worker) — the bottom tier is User, not Worker.
Option D (Administrator, Manager, and User) — there is no "Administrator" partner role; the platform creates Executive at the top.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Q57 had no options and "Executive, Manager, and User" as the correct field; built the choice set and tidied the stem.

question: (Variant) Susan posts a file to the Chatter feed for a record of an object which OWD is private. Which two statements accurately describe who can view the file by default? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Susan and users with the View All Data permission.
optionB: Susan and users with access to the record.
optionC: Susan and users with a shared chatter post link to the file.
optionD: Susan only.
explanation:
Susan and users with the View All Data permission, and Susan and users with access to the record, are the two accurate statements. Posting a file to a record's feed puts it in the "Privately Shared" state, and Salesforce spells out who that reaches: "Only the file owner, users with Modify All Data or View All Data permission, and specific file viewers can find and view this file." Records are among the entities that pick up viewer permission — "Groups (including group members) and records have viewer permission for files posted to their feeds" — so anyone with access to the record can see the file.
The record's Private org-wide default limits who can see the file through the record, but the org-wide View All Data permission reaches it independently.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Susan and users with a shared chatter post link) — link sharing is a separate way of making a file privately shared, not a precondition for this one; no link is required.
Option D (Susan only) — the file is not restricted to Susan alone; record viewers and View All Data users can see it.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sf.collab_files_settings_perms.htm&type=5

question: Universal Containers created a custom object called Defect and would like to enable the Sharing button on the Defect page layout to share the records manually to other users in the organization. In which scenario will the Sharing button appear?
optionA: The Sharing model is either Private or Public Read only.
optionB: The Sharing button always appears.
optionC: The Sharing model is Public Read/Write.
optionD: The Sharing model is Public Read/Write/Transfer.
explanation:
The Sharing model being either Private or Public Read Only is the scenario in which the Sharing button appears. Manual sharing makes sense only when there is access to grant, so the button shows only when the object's OWD is more restrictive than Public Read/Write.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (The Sharing button always appears) — it is hidden whenever the OWD already gives everyone full access.
Option C (The Sharing model is Public Read/Write) — under Public Read/Write everyone already has read and edit, so there is nothing to share and the button is not shown.
Option D (The Sharing model is Public Read/Write/Transfer) — even more open than Public Read/Write; the button is not shown.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.granting_access_to_records_lex.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A custom ServiceFeedback object is used to collect partner feedback. ServiceFeedback records should be available to all internal employees. The OWD is set to Private for external users so partners cannot see feedback from other partner users. How can the Architect give access to all internal employees?
optionA: Create a trigger on ServiceFeedback to change ownership to an internal employee.
optionB: Ensure all the internal users are above the partners in the role hierarchy.
optionC: Create an Owner based sharing rule for all ServiceFeedback records owned by Partners.
optionD: Set OWD, for Internal Users to Public Read Only.
explanation:
Setting the OWD for Internal Users to Public Read Only is how the Architect gives access to all internal employees. With separate internal and external OWD, you can keep external (partner) access Private so partners cannot see each other's feedback while setting the internal OWD to Public Read Only so all employees can read every ServiceFeedback record.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a trigger to change ownership to an internal employee) — moves ownership away from the partner for no reason and still only gives one employee access, not all of them.
Option B (Ensure all internal users are above the partners in the role hierarchy) — the hierarchy cannot put every employee above every partner account's roles, and it is unnecessary when the split OWD solves it directly.
Option C (an Owner based sharing rule for records owned by Partners) — workable but redundant; a sharing rule per partner-owned set is extra configuration when the internal OWD already does the job.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has implemented Customer Community with customer community plus license for its distributors. Retail distributors have part-time agents who work for multiple distributors. Those agents should have access to other distributor accounts as well. What can be configured to grant agents access to different distributor accounts?
optionA: Use Apex sharing to share distributor accounts with agents using the Account__ Share table.
optionB: Use share group to share distributor accounts with agents who have account contact relationship.
optionC: Create sharing rules to share distributor accounts with agents.
optionD: Create sharing set to share distributor accounts with agents using account contact relationship.
explanation:
Creating a sharing set to share distributor accounts with agents using the account contact relationship is what can be configured. A sharing set handles the multi-account case directly, and it is the documented mechanism for exactly this shape of problem. Create a Sharing Set for Experience Cloud Site Users covers it: "If you created a user from a contact to multiple accounts, you can grant access to all records with a lookup to any accounts related to that contact. Select Contact.RelatedAccount and Account respectively, and make sure that the relevant account-contact relationships are active."
That is the part-time agent scenario. The agent is one contact related to several distributor accounts through Contacts to Multiple Accounts, and Account is itself an available object in a sharing set, so the access mapping grants each agent the distributor accounts their contact is actively related to. Adding or removing an account-contact relationship changes access with no code.
Note that share groups — a different feature — are the thing unavailable to Customer Community Plus and Partner Community licences. Sharing sets themselves are available.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Apex sharing via the AccountShare table) — would also work, but it is a code solution to a problem the platform already solves declaratively, and it has to be maintained as agents move between distributors.
Option B (a share group with agents who have an account contact relationship) — share groups are unavailable to Customer Community Plus and Partner Community licences, and they share records owned by site users with internal users, not accounts with agents.
Option C (sharing rules to share distributor accounts with agents) — ordinary sharing rules cannot target community users on a per-account basis.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_license_types_communities.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer moved from Apex sharing to the sharing set. The previous explanation claimed a sharing set keyed on the account-contact relationship "only covers the agent's own account"; the sharing-set documentation says the opposite, naming Contact.RelatedAccount as the mapping for a contact related to multiple accounts.

question: Universal Containers has developed an AppExchange managed package for their distribution partners, which required a private key to be generated for each partner and used by the code. Universal Containers support representatives must be able to access the private key value to debug connection issues, but it must not be possible for the partner to access the value. How can the Architect best support this requirement?
optionA: Store the value in a text field on a protected custom setting in the package.
optionB: Store the value in a static variable in a class included in the managed package.
optionC: Store the value in the text field on a list custom setting in the managed package.
optionD: Store the value in an encrypted field on a custom object in the package.
explanation:
Storing the value in an encrypted field on a custom object in the package is how the Architect best supports this. The discriminator here is that support representatives must be able to read the value, not merely that partners must not. An encrypted field on a packaged custom object keeps the value retrievable while masking it by default: only users with the View Encrypted Data permission see the plain text, and it is masked for everyone else. Grant that permission to the support profile and withhold it from partner profiles and both halves of the requirement are met.
Worth stating plainly, because the protection is only as good as the permission hygiene: whoever administers the subscriber org can in principle assign View Encrypted Data, so this design relies on that permission being controlled. Where the value must never be readable by the subscriber at all, protected custom settings or protected custom metadata in a managed package are the stronger option — which is why the related "how do I secure callout credentials" item keys those instead.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a text field on a protected custom setting in the package) — in a managed package a protected custom setting is reachable only by Apex inside that package and namespace, and the subscriber cannot read it at all, which hides the key from support staff working in the partner org just as effectively as from the partner.
Option B (a static variable in a class in the managed package) — not stored data you can look at later, and a hard-coded value cannot differ per partner.
Option C (a text field on a list custom setting in the managed package) — a list custom setting protects nothing; the partner's admins can read it in Setup.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.cs_schema_settings.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.fields_about_encrypted_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.custommetadatatypes_package_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has created a custom object to store highly confidential client relationship data with Private sharing settings. Which two options would an Architect choose to ensure access only to the record owner and the administrator? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Disable "Grant Access Using Hierarchies."
optionB: Disable the "Create" permission on all other profiles.
optionC: Disable the "Read" permission on all other profiles.
optionD: Disable the "View All" permission on all other profiles.
explanation:
Disabling "Grant Access Using Hierarchies" and disabling the "View All" permission on all other profiles are the two options. To restrict a Private custom object to only the owner and the administrator, switch off hierarchy inheritance so managers do not inherit access, and remove View All from other profiles so no one else can read all records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Disable the "Create" permission on all other profiles) — removes the owners' own ability to create their records, and does nothing about who can read existing ones.
Option C (Disable the "Read" permission on all other profiles) — would also remove the owner's own ability to see their records; the requirement is to keep owner access.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_view_all_mod_all.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a customer that meets criteria for two Enterprise territory Management territories (Portugal and Southern Europe). What is necessary to assign opportunities to a territory for this account?
optionA: Create a criteria-based sharing rule on the Opportunity to assign It to a territory.
optionB: Create a Process Builder Process that updates the Territory field on the Opportunity
optionC: The territory with the highest Territory Type Priority is automatically assigned to the Opportunity
optionD: Create an Apex class that implement. Filter-Based Opportunity Territory Assignment
explanation:
Creating an Apex class that implements Filter-Based Opportunity Territory Assignment is what is necessary. When an account qualifies for multiple ETM territories, opportunities are not automatically assigned to a single territory; you must implement the Apex class for Filter-Based Opportunity Territory Assignment to decide.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a criteria-based sharing rule on the Opportunity) — sharing rules grant access; they do not populate the Territory field on an opportunity.
Option B (a Process Builder Process that updates the Territory field) — Process Builder is retired and was never the documented mechanism; ETM provides the filter-based assignment hook for exactly this.
Option C (the highest Territory Type Priority is automatically assigned) — false, and it was the source's answer: priority only feeds the Apex logic rather than assigning on its own.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.tm2_enable_ota.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a Performance Feedback custom object (Private organization-wide default) used by customers to report any Issues with delivery drivers. Feedback should not be visible to the driver, but any feedback records should be accessible to people above them in the Role Hierarchy, even when the driver changes managers. Assuming managers have Read access to the Feedback object, which three steps are necessary to solve these requirements?
optionA: Remove Read permission on the Driver profile, have feedback ownership transferred to the driver's manager when feedback Is submitted, and use the Role Hierarchy to give access to a driver's manager.
optionB: Remove Read permission on the Driver profile, have feedback ownership transferred to the driver when feedback is submitted, and use the Role Hierarchy to give access to a driver's manager.
optionC: Remove Read permission on the Driver profile, have feedback ownership transferred to the driver when feedback is submitted, and create an ownership-based sharing rule,
explanation:
Removing Read permission on the Driver profile, having feedback ownership transferred to the driver when feedback is submitted, and using the Role Hierarchy to give access to a driver's manager are the three steps. Keeping the driver as owner means the dynamic Role Hierarchy always routes access to whoever is currently above them, and removing Read on the Driver profile means the owner still cannot see it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (transfer ownership to the driver's manager) — loses the driver linkage, and access no longer follows the driver when they change managers.
Option C (transfer to the driver and create an ownership-based sharing rule) — the source's answer, but a sharing rule is static: it shares to a fixed role or group and breaks when the manager changes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What should a Salesforce architect recommend to make sure that users that gained access to a custom of sharing do not lose access to it when its owner is changed?
optionA: Create a specific Sharing Reason for the custom object.
optionB: Use ''runAS'' system method in Apex classes to enforce record visibility.
optionC: Create a new record in the Share object with RowCause "Manual".
optionD: Use ''With Sharing'' keyword to make sure record visibility will be considered
explanation:
Creating a specific Sharing Reason for the custom object is what the architect should recommend. Apex managed sharing rows tagged with a custom Apex Sharing Reason are preserved when record ownership changes, whereas Manual row-cause shares are deleted on owner change.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Use "runAs" system method in Apex classes to enforce record visibility) — runAs is a test-only method and has nothing to do with whether a share row persists.
Option C (Create a new record in the Share object with RowCause "Manual") — a Manual share is exactly what gets deleted when the owner changes.
Option D (Use "With Sharing" keyword) — controls whether code respects sharing; it does not affect share-row persistence.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/latest/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_record_access_under_the_hood.pdf

question: Universal Containers has a custom object, Employee Review, with an Organization-Wide Default security setting of Private. A user lookup on the Employee Review object is populated when a reviewer is assigned to perform a review. How can this user be granted edit access to the record if they are not the owner?
optionA: The user will be granted access to the record automatically when the user lookup is populated.
optionB: Create a workflow rule to share the Employee Review record with the user in the lookup field.
optionC: Create an Apex trigger to insert an Employee Review Share record with an access level of Edit.
optionD: Create a criteria-based sharing rule to share the record with the user in the lookup field.
explanation:
Creating an Apex trigger to insert an Employee Review Share record with an access level of Edit is how the user gets edit access. A user named in a lookup needs edit access on a private record, which requires programmatic Apex managed sharing; the trigger inserts a share row at access level Edit for that user.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (access is granted automatically when the lookup is populated) — populating a lookup does not grant any access; the user is only referenced.
Option B (a workflow rule to share the record) — workflow cannot create share records.
Option D (a criteria-based sharing rule to the user in the lookup) — criteria-based rules share to roles and groups; they cannot target the arbitrary user named in a lookup field on each record.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Assuming granular locking is enabled, what activity can happen in parallel to changing a community account owner without risking group membership lock errors?
optionA: Deletion of a Role
optionB: Creation of a Role
optionC: Creation of a Territory
optionD: Deletion of a Territory
explanation:
Creation of a Territory is the activity that can happen in parallel. Salesforce publishes the concurrency matrix for granular locking, and the row for this scenario is unambiguous: "Changing customer or partner account owner — Territory creation." That single entry is the whole answer; territory creation is the only listed operation that can proceed alongside it.
Changing the owner of a customer or partner account is a form of role reparenting — the partner account's roles move to a new parent — and reparenting still blocks almost all other group updates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Deletion of a Role) — appears elsewhere in the table but not in this row; it is blocked by the role reparenting an owner change implies.
Option B (Creation of a Role) — likewise not listed as concurrent with an account owner change.
Option D (Deletion of a Territory) — not in this row either; only territory creation is.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

question: A banking company wants their customers Date of Birth Field searchable by Banking Reps, but only editable by Customer Support Reps. Which approach is recommended to meet this requirement?
optionA: Create a Validation rule on the Date of Birth field so the rule returns true only when user.profilename matches Customer Support Rep.
optionB: Set the Field-Level Security for the Date of Birth field to be Visible to the Customer Support Rep profile, and set the Date of Birth field Visible and Read-Only to the Banking Rep profile.
optionC: Add Date of Birth field to the Search layout of the Contact Object. Modify the Page layout assigned to Customer Support Rep and add Date of Birth field as Required.
explanation:
Setting the Field-Level Security for Date of Birth to Visible for Customer Support Reps, and Visible and Read-Only for Banking Reps, is the recommended approach. Field-Level Security is the declarative way to make the field searchable and visible to Banking Reps as read-only while keeping it editable for Customer Support Reps.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a Validation rule that returns true only for Customer Support Rep) — a validation rule blocks save but does not cleanly control visibility and edit, and it fires on every save of the record, not just edits to that field.
Option C (add the field to the Search layout and make it Required on the Support Rep layout) — search and page layouts do not restrict who may edit the field; Banking Reps could still change it wherever it appears.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
