question: When you make changes to roles and groups, Salesforce locks the entire group membership table, which makes it impossible to process group changes in multiple threads to increase throughput on updates. Which feature should be enabled to address this?
optionA: Deferred Sharing Maintenance
optionB: Granular Locking
optionC: Parallel Sharing Rule Recalculation
optionD: Implicit Sharing
explanation:
Granular Locking is the feature to enable. It replaces the single lock over the entire group-membership table with locks scoped to the parts of the membership graph actually being touched, which is what allows concurrent processing. Salesforce lists the benefits: groups in separate hierarchies can be manipulated concurrently, public groups and roles that do not include territories are not blocked by territory operations, users can be added to territories and public groups at the same time, and user provisioning can run in parallel.
Note that granular locking is enabled by default in current orgs — the stem describes the pre-granular-locking behaviour.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Deferred Sharing Maintenance) — suspends recalculation for a planned window rather than parallelising it.
Option C (Parallel Sharing Rule Recalculation) — speeds up sharing-rule recalculation specifically, not group-membership updates.
Option D (Implicit Sharing) — built-in record access between accounts and their children, not a concurrency control.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_locking.htm

corrected.note: Q71 had no options and "Granular Locking" as the correct field; turned the statement into a question and built the choice set.

question: A user at Universal Containers would like to give access to a Report folder to someone else in the organization. Which two access permissions should the user have to support this requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The "Viewer" Report folder permission
optionB: The "Editor" Report folder permission.
optionC: The "Manage Reports in Public Folders" Profile permission.
optionD: The "Manager" Report folder permission.
explanation:
The "Manage Reports in Public Folders" profile permission and the "Manager" report folder permission are the two the user needs. Giving someone else access to a report folder requires the profile permission plus the folder-level Manager access that allows sharing the folder.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (The "Viewer" Report folder permission) — Viewers can run and see the folder's content but cannot grant other users access to it.
Option B (The "Editor" Report folder permission) — Editors can add and change content but still cannot share the folder; only Manager access can.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.access_report_folders.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.analytics_sharing_permissions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a business unit that uses a custom object to track requests which demands a high level of internal team collaboration. Although all requests must have an owner, all employees are required to collaborate on requests. Which recommendation should a Salesforce architect provide to optimize the solution and meet these requirements?
optionA: Set the Request object's OWD to Public Read/Write.
optionB: Set the Request object's OWD to Private and grant Modify All Data permission on all Profiles for the Request object.
optionC: Set the Request object's OWD to Private and criteria-based sharing rule to share all Request records with all internal users.
optionD: Set the Request object's OWD to Public Read Only and configure role hierarchy.
explanation:
Setting the Request object's OWD to Public Read/Write is the recommendation. When every employee must read and edit requests while each record still has an owner, the simplest optimal model is an open OWD, which retains ownership but lets all users collaborate.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Private OWD plus Modify All Data on all profiles) — Modify All Data over-grants across the platform, and a Private default that is immediately overridden for everyone is the wrong shape.
Option C (Private OWD plus a criteria-based rule to all internal users) — heavier than simply opening the OWD: a rule that shares everything to everyone is an OWD in disguise, with a recalculation cost attached.
Option D (Public Read Only plus role hierarchy) — read-only lets employees see requests but not edit them, and the hierarchy only extends access upward, so peers still cannot collaborate.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two access grants are stored in the Group Maintenance tables? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Inherited access grants
optionB: Explicit grants
optionC: Group Membership grants
optionD: Implicit grants
explanation:
Inherited access grants and Group Membership grants are the two stored in the Group Maintenance tables. Salesforce uses four types of access grant — explicit, group membership, inherited and implicit — and splits them across two families of table. Record-Level Access: Under the Hood defines the Group Maintenance tables as "Tables that store the data supporting group membership and inherited access grants".
The division of labour is worth holding onto: the Object Sharing table records grants made to a particular user or group on a particular record, while the Group Maintenance tables record who belongs to which group and who therefore inherits from whom. A query joins the two — record id against Object Sharing, then user or group id against Group Maintenance — so an explicit grant to one user resolves at runtime into access for everyone above them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Explicit grants) — live in the Object Sharing table, as share rows on the record.
Option D (Implicit grants) — maintained by the system on the objects themselves, not in the Group Maintenance tables.
References:
https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/latest/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_record_access_under_the_hood.pdf

question: Universal Containers (UC) has 200 distributors that use Partner Community Licenses. Partners cannot see each other's data, but UC is also trying to give more visibility to certain individuals at a distributor. Which scalable solution would an architect recommend that will give users in the partner manager role access to all Case and Container records owned by other partner managers and partner users (but not the partner executive) at the same distributor?
optionA: Create Sharing sets.
optionB: Create a permission set granting the View All permission to Case and Container records.
optionC: Give Super User permission to the partner manager users.
optionD: Create ownership-based sharing rules for your distributors.
explanation:
Giving Super User permission to the partner manager users is the scalable solution. Super user access is the feature built for this, and it scales because it is granted per user rather than configured per distributor. Salesforce describes it for Partner Community licences as letting a user "get insights into the records of other partner users who are at their role level or below them in the account role hierarchy", covering cases, leads, custom objects and opportunities.
That maps onto the requirement exactly. Each partner account has its own Partner User, Partner Manager and Partner Executive hierarchy, so a partner manager with super user access reaches records owned by other partner managers and by partner users at the same distributor, and stops short of the partner executive above them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Create Sharing sets) — sharing sets grant access based on a lookup to the user's own account or contact; they cannot express "records owned by peers at my role and below".
Option B (a permission set granting View All on Case and Container) — would expose every case and container in the org rather than one distributor's.
Option D (ownership-based sharing rules for your distributors) — would need one rule per distributor across 200 accounts, and cannot be aimed at a partner account's own roles.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_super_user_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has requirement to integrate Salesforce with an external system to control record access. What option should the Architect consider when designing a solution?
optionA: Use the Security API to modify the role hierarchy in Salesforce.
optionB: Use the SOAP API to maintain the related SObject_share records.
optionC: Use the Metadata API to maintain the related SObject records.
optionD: Use the SOAP API to create new Criteria-Based Sharing Rules in Salesforce.
explanation:
Using the SOAP API to maintain the related SObject_share records is the option to consider. An external integration that controls record access maintains the share tables directly, which is done through the SOAP API on the object's share records such as AccountShare.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Use the Security API to modify the role hierarchy) — there is no "Security API", and reshaping the role hierarchy is not how an external system grants access to individual records.
Option C (Use the Metadata API to maintain the related SObject records) — the Metadata API handles configuration and metadata rather than data rows.
Option D (Use the SOAP API to create new Criteria-Based Sharing Rules) — sharing rules are metadata, not per-record grants; you cannot create per-record criteria rules through the data API for this need.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The sales manager in Japan have asked the sales manager in Australia to assist them with closing their deals. How are these requirements achieved?
optionA: Use sharing set to give the sales manager access to the deals.
optionB: Create ownership-based sharing rule.
optionC: Use opportunity teams to automatically add the sales manager as a team member.
optionD: Assign the sales manager View All on the opportunity object.
explanation:
Creating an ownership-based sharing rule is how the requirement is achieved. The Australia manager needs access to the Japan team's deals, so a rule sharing opportunities owned by the Japan managers to the Australia manager grants it declaratively.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a sharing set) — sharing sets are an Experience Cloud site mechanism for external users, not for internal managers.
Option C (opportunity teams to automatically add the manager) — arguably cleaner for purely ad-hoc help, and worth noting, but there is no automatic team membership across owners without configuring a default team on every Japan rep.
Option D (View All on the opportunity object) — over-grants: the Australia manager would see every opportunity in the org, not just Japan's.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US

question:
Universal Containers (UC) has a private Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD) model for the Account object and needs to control the access of records and fields according to these requirements:
* Sales reps can view/edit only their own records and cannot access the field "segment" in account page.
* Service reps need to view all accounts but cannot edit any information.
* Sales managers can modify any account of reps reporting to them.
* Service managers can modify any account.
How can a Salesforce architect provide an optimal solution for this scenario?
optionA: Use profiles, sharing rules, and change OWD to public read-only.
optionB: Use profiles, manual sharing, and field-level security.
optionC: Use profiles, permission sets, and field-level security.
optionD: Use profiles, permission sets, role hierarchy, and field-level security.
explanation:
Using profiles, permission sets, role hierarchy, and field-level security is the optimal solution. The mixed requirements of own versus all, edit versus view, manager-modifies-reports, and hiding a field require the full stack: profiles and permission sets for object access, role hierarchy for the manager-edit rule, and Field-Level Security to hide the segment field.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (profiles, sharing rules, and OWD public read-only) — a public read-only OWD lets sales reps see every account, contradicting "own records only", and nothing here hides the segment field.
Option B (profiles, manual sharing, and field-level security) — manual sharing is per record and cannot deliver the manager-modifies-reports rule at scale.
Option C (profiles, permission sets, and field-level security) — omits the role hierarchy, so sales managers gain no access to the accounts of the reps reporting to them.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers regularly uploads large amounts of parent and child records into Salesforce to maintain integrations with other systems that update their date in scheduled batches, or continuously in real time. Which two situations may pose a risk of producing locking errors? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Updates to child records that have the same parent records are being processed simultaneously in separate transactions.
optionB: Updates to parent and child records are being processed in the same batch.
optionC: Updates to parent records and their child records being processed simultaneously in separate threads.
optionD: Updates to parent and child records are being processed synchronously in the same threads.
explanation:
Updates to child records sharing the same parent processed simultaneously in separate transactions, and updates to parent records and their children processed simultaneously in separate threads, are the two risky situations. Lock contention arises when related parent and child rows are updated concurrently in separate transactions or threads, because Salesforce locks the parent during the child's sharing and rollup operations.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (parent and child updates in the same batch) — processing them together serializes the work and avoids the lock.
Option D (parent and child updates synchronously in the same thread) — likewise serial: one thread cannot contend with itself for the parent lock.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_record_level_locking.htm

question: A dummy user at Universal Containers owns more that 10,000 lead records. The system assigned all these leads to a dummy user. This is causing performance issues whenever role hierarchy changes. Which two options should be recommended to improve performance? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Assign ownership to a small number of users.
optionB: Add the dummy user into a public group.
optionC: Add the dummy user to the bottom of the role hierarchy.
optionD: Do not assign a role to the dummy user.
explanation:
Assigning ownership to a small number of users and not assigning a role to the dummy user are the two keyed recommendations. Ownership data skew is "when a single user owns more than 10,000 records of an object", and Salesforce gives two remedies for the parked-leads pattern in this stem. The first is to spread the records: "Distributing ownership of records across a greater number of users decreases the chance of long-running updates occurring." The second is the one that applies when you must keep a dummy owner: "If you do have a compelling reason for assigning ownership to a small number of users, you can minimize possible performance impacts by not assigning the users to a role" — which is option D exactly.
Option A is the intended "spread the ownership out" answer, but read it as printed and it says the opposite of the documentation, which names assigning ownership to a small number of users as the risky configuration rather than the fix. Treat A as loosely worded rather than as a rule to memorise.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Add the dummy user into a public group) — Salesforce says to keep skewed owners out of public groups that can be the source of a sharing rule, so this makes things worse.
Option C (Add the dummy user to the bottom of the role hierarchy) — backwards: where such a user must have a role, the guidance is a separate role at the top of the hierarchy, left there.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_group_membership_data_skew.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands, but option A as printed inverts the documented remedy — Salesforce prescribes distributing ownership across a greater number of users and describes "assigning ownership to a small number of users" as the condition that causes skew. The old explanation read A as "distributing ownership across many users", which is not what the option says.

question: Universal Container (UC) wants all full-time internal employees to be able to view all leads. A subset of employees should also be able to see leads. Which organization default (OWD) approach should an architect recommend that will help US implement these requirement?
optionA: Implement a Public Read/write OWD on Lead
optionB: Implement a Public Read only OWD on Lead
optionC: Implement a Public Read/write/Transfer OWD on Lead.
optionD: Implement a Private OWD on Lead.
explanation:
Implementing a Public Read Only OWD on Lead is the approach to recommend. It gives every internal employee visibility of every lead while keeping edit rights with the owner, which is the baseline this requirement needs. A subset can then be granted edit through sharing rules layered on top — org-wide defaults set the floor, and sharing rules are the exceptions that open access further.
(The stem looks garbled: its second sentence repeats "see leads" where the requirement it is contrasting must be edit access. Read it as "a subset of employees should also be able to edit leads" — that is the only reading on which the four options differ meaningfully.)
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Public Read/write OWD on Lead) — hands edit to the whole org, which over-grants beyond the subset.
Option C (Public Read/write/Transfer OWD on Lead) — hands edit and transfer to the whole org, over-granting further.
Option D (Private OWD on Lead) — hides leads from everyone but their owners, the opposite of "all employees can view all leads".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has set Account Sharing to Private with Account Teams enabled. Which two user groups can add team members on the Account? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: The current Account Owner can add team members.
optionB: The user specified as the Manager on the Owner's User record
optionC: Someone above the Account Owner in the Role Hierarchy with read access
optionD: Any Account Team Member with read access on the Account
explanation:
The current Account Owner, and someone above the Account Owner in the Role Hierarchy with read access, are the two user groups that can add team members.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (The user specified as the Manager on the Owner's User record) — the user record's Manager field is irrelevant to sharing; it confers no rights over the owner's accounts.
Option D (Any Account Team Member with read access) — existing team members cannot add others; only the owner and those above the owner in the hierarchy manage the team.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question:
Universal Containers has the following requirements:
* The Commercial Account and Consumer Account support departments should not collaborate.
* The Commercial and Consumer sales users roll up to the same VP of Sales, but there should be no collaboration between sales departments.
* The Commercial sales department should share its customers with the Commercial support department.
* The Consumer sales department shares its customers with the Consumer support department.
* The Commercial and Consumer support departments roll up to the same Support Director.
* The sales departments will remain the Account Owner for the Accounts that they sell to.
What is the recommended Org-Wide Sharing Default for Accounts, and how would the Architect enable proper Commercial and Consumer Sales to Support Account Sharing for this scenario?
optionA: Private Account Sharing with Sharing Rules from Commercial Sales Role(s) to Consumer Support Role(s) and Consumer Sales Role(s) to Commercial Support Role(s).
optionB: Private Account Sharing with Sharing Rules from Commercial support Role(s) to Commercial Support Role(s) and Consumer Sales Role(s) to Consumer Support Role(s).
optionC: Read-Only Account Sharing with Sharing Rules from Commercial Sales Role(s) to Consumer Support Group(s) and Consumer Sales Role(s) to Commercial Support Groups(s).
optionD: Private Account Sharing with Sharing Rules from Commercial Sales Group(s) to Commercial Support Groups(s) and Consumer Sales Group(s) to Consumer Support Group(s).
explanation:
Private Account Sharing with Sharing Rules from Commercial Sales Groups to Commercial Support Groups and Consumer Sales Groups to Consumer Support Groups is the recommendation. The sales departments stay owners under a Private model, and group-to-group sharing rules mapping each Sales group to its matching Support group give each support team only its own department's accounts with no cross-collaboration.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Commercial Sales to Consumer Support and Consumer Sales to Commercial Support) — cross-matched: each support department would receive the other department's accounts.
Option B (Commercial support Roles to Commercial Support Roles and Consumer Sales to Consumer Support) — the first rule shares support to itself rather than from Commercial Sales, so the commercial mapping is missing.
Option C (Read-Only Account Sharing with cross-matched rules) — a Read-Only OWD lets every department see every account, defeating the no-collaboration requirement, and the rules are cross-matched as well.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has created a public group with certain Sales Engineers to help on complex deals and a sharing rule to grant access to these opportunities. Opportunity OWD is private. What is the impact of these sharing settings?
optionA: Subordinates of Managers who have Sales Engineers in the public group will also have access to these records.
optionB: Sales Engineers that have a similar role of the Sales Engineers of the public group will also have access to these records.
optionC: Sales Engineers Managers and their managers in the role hierarchy will also have access to these records.
optionD: Sales Engineers direct reports will also have access to these records.
explanation:
Sales Engineers' managers and their managers in the role hierarchy will also have access to these records. Sharing to a public group grants access to the group's members and, through the Role Hierarchy, to users above those members, so the managers up the chain gain access to the opportunities.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Subordinates of the Managers will also have access) — access flows up the hierarchy, not down; subordinates do not inherit a group-based share.
Option B (Sales Engineers with a similar role) — a similar role is not membership; peers outside the group gain nothing.
Option D (Sales Engineers' direct reports) — reports sit below the members, and hierarchy access only flows upward.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has recently activated an integration that synchronizes customer information and orders into their CRM of choice: Salesforce.com. One of their largest customers, United Air, has over 12,000 unique contacts. Since the integration was activated, sales reps are having trouble adding contacts to the United Air account. When a sales rep adds a contact, they get the following error message: UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW, this issue seems to affect the United Air account and several other large customers. The sales rep can usually save the contact by trying again later in the evening. What should the Architect recommend as a possible solution?
optionA: Add a role-based sharing rule so all sales team members have Read/Write access to contacts.
optionB: Remove sharing rules and replace them with Apex sharing for Unite Air and the other large accounts.
optionC: Implement an account hierarchy and redistribute the contacts evenly under the child accounts.
optionD: Create a permission set for the sales team to grant them Read/Write access to all account fields.
explanation:
Implementing an account hierarchy and redistributing the contacts evenly under child accounts is the possible solution to recommend. The UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW error on a 12,000-contact account is parent (lookup) data skew, where too many child contacts under one account cause lock contention; spreading the contacts across child accounts relieves it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a role-based sharing rule giving Read/Write on contacts) — sharing changes do not address the parent-row lock taken when a child is inserted.
Option B (replace sharing rules with Apex sharing for the large accounts) — likewise leaves the single skewed parent in place; the lock is on the account row, not on how it is shared.
Option D (a permission set granting Read/Write to all account fields) — field access has nothing to do with row locking.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_parent_child_data_skew.htm

question: At Universal Containers, users should only see Accounts they or their subordinates own. All Accounts with the custom field "Kay Customer" should be visible to all Senior Account Managers. There is a custom field on the Account record that contains sensitive information and should be hidden from all users, except 3 designated users who require view and edit access. These three users come from different user groups, and will change occasionally. Which three platform security features are required to support these requirements with the minimum amount of effort? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Criteria-Based Sharing Rules
optionB: Owner-Based Sharing Rules
optionC: Role Hierarchy
optionD: Apex Managed Sharing
explanation:
Criteria-Based Sharing Rules, Role Hierarchy, and Permission Sets are the three features. The owner-or-subordinates visibility comes from the Role Hierarchy under a Private model, the Key Customer visibility for all Senior Account Managers is a criteria-based sharing rule, and the sensitive field for three rotating cross-group users is best handled with a Permission Set granting FLS.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Owner-Based Sharing Rules) — nothing in the requirements is keyed on who owns the record; the Key Customer rule is criteria-based.
Option D (Apex Managed Sharing) — code where declarative features already cover every requirement, so it is not the minimum-effort choice.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.security_sharing_rules_criteria.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is a fast-growing company that sells containers globally. It has thousands of dealerships throughout the world where local dealers service Containers sold locally. They recently opened two dealerships in California: NorthCal and SoCal. Universal Containers implemented a new partner community to enable their dealers. Each dealership has a dealer Manager who has all service agents report into them. Assuming a private sharing model, what is the best option to enable dealer managers to have visibility to customer cases within their dealership and not across all dealerships?
optionA: Create sharing groups that share all cases to all agents under the Dealer manager.
optionB: Create a batch job that creates sharing rules as needed, based on the cases created.
optionC: Build a trigger that create manual sharing of cases as needed whenever a new case is created.
optionD: No changes are needed to the sharing and visibility model to implement this requirement.
explanation:
No changes are needed to the sharing and visibility model to implement this requirement. In a private partner community, the dealer manager already sits above their service agents in the Role Hierarchy per dealership, so cases owned by agents are visible to their own manager and not across dealerships with no extra configuration.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sharing groups that share all cases to all agents under the Dealer manager) — redundant given the hierarchy, and it shares cases to agents rather than to the manager the stem asks about.
Option B (a batch job that creates sharing rules as needed) — sharing rules are metadata, not something a batch job should mint per case, and the hierarchy already delivers the access.
Option C (a trigger that creates manual sharing whenever a new case is created) — code to reproduce what the partner role hierarchy does for free.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales Reps at Universal Containers sometimes create large files as a part of the Sales process that are too large to share over email. They would like users to be able to share files with customers, but the CISO has requested that any file links shared must be protected by a password. How can this be accomplished?
optionA: Set up an experience cloud site for customers to access files. Share the file with customers via chatter. Customers can then log into the site to access the content.
optionB: Sales reps can create a content delivery. During creation, the user should select the option to require a password to access content.
optionC: Utilize an AppExchange product for delivering password-protected files to their customers,
explanation:
Sales reps creating a content delivery and selecting the option to require a password is how this is accomplished. Salesforce Content Delivery lets a rep generate a shareable link for a large file and, at creation, require a password to access it, meeting the CISO's requirement natively.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Experience Cloud site where customers log in to access files shared via Chatter) — heavier than needed, and a site login is not a per-file password on a shared link.
Option C (an AppExchange product for password-protected files) — unnecessary for a capability the platform already provides.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.content_delivery_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A sales rep at Universal Containers (UC) has manually shared an Opportunity record with internal Pre-Sales users. After some time, the sales rep moved to another position and all opportunities records that were owned were transferred to a new sales rep. What happened to the internal Pre-Sales users' access to the opportunity?
optionA: They still have access to the record due to inherited sharing.
optionB: They still have access to the record due to implicit sharing.
optionC: They will no longer have access to the record.
optionD: They still have access to the record due to team access.
explanation:
They will no longer have access to the record. A manual share is deleted when record ownership changes, so when the opportunity is transferred to a new rep the Pre-Sales users' manually granted access is removed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (still have access due to inherited sharing) — inherited access comes through the role hierarchy or group membership; the Pre-Sales users were granted access by a manual share, which does not survive the transfer.
Option B (still have access due to implicit sharing) — implicit sharing is the built-in parent-child access between accounts and their children; it did not create this share.
Option D (still have access due to team access) — they were never on an opportunity team; a manual share is not team membership.
References:
https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/latest/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/salesforce_record_access_under_the_hood.pdf
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers would like to create a custom team solution that can be used on a custom Loan object. The following requirements must be met: The Loan custom object should be set to Private in the Org-Wide Defaults. Any user added to the Custom Team object should have Read Only access to the corresponding Loan record. If the Custom Team record is marked as "Primary" then the corresponding user should have Read/Edit access to the corresponding Loan record. Which two methods will allow the Architect to meet the requirements? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Create a custom trigger on the Custom Team object that inserts or updates records in the Loan_share object.
optionB: Create a criteria-based sharing rule on the Loan object that will share the Loan record with the appropriate user in the Custom Team object.
optionC: Create Apex Sharing Reasons on the Loan object to identify the reason the Loan record was share.
optionD: Create an owner-based sharing rule on the Custom Team object that will share the Loan record to the owner of the Custom Team record.
explanation:
Creating a custom trigger on the Custom Team object that inserts or updates Loan_share records, and creating Apex Sharing Reasons on the Loan object, are the two methods. Differential access of Read for members and Read/Edit for the Primary record on a private object requires Apex managed sharing: the trigger writes Loan share rows at the correct access level, and Apex Sharing Reasons identify and maintain those shares and preserve them on owner change.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a criteria-based sharing rule on the Loan object) — a rule cannot read the related Custom Team record's Primary flag per record, nor share to an arbitrary user named on a child record.
Option D (an owner-based sharing rule on the Custom Team object) — shares Custom Team records, not Loan records, and targets the team record's owner rather than the user it names.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers would like to restrict users' access to export reports. What option supports this requirement?
optionA: Remove the "Report Manager" user permission.
optionB: Remove the Export button from the report page layout.
optionC: Remove "Allow Export" on the report folder settings.
optionD: Remove the "Export Reports" profile permission.
explanation:
Removing the "Export Reports" profile permission is the option that supports this. Restricting report export is governed by that permission, so removing it stops users from exporting. This corrects the source.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Remove the "Report Manager" user permission) — there is no such user permission governing export.
Option B (Remove the Export button from the report page layout) — the source's answer, but reports have no page layouts, so the button does not exist to remove.
Option C (Remove "Allow Export" on the report folder settings) — there is no "Allow Export" folder setting.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.analytics_sharing_permissions.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which two reasons should the Architect consider regarding the use of Apex Sharing Reasons? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Ensuring the developer can more easily troubleshoot programmatic sharing.
optionB: Ensuring the Share record is not deleted upon ownership change.
optionC: Ensuring the Share record is deleted upon ownership change.
optionD: Ensuring there is additional criteria available for Criteria-Based Sharing.
explanation:
Ensuring the developer can more easily troubleshoot programmatic sharing, and ensuring the Share record is not deleted upon ownership change, are the two reasons. Apex Sharing Reasons label programmatic shares so developers can identify why a record was shared, and shares created with a custom reason are retained when ownership changes, unlike Manual shares.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Ensuring the Share record is deleted upon ownership change) — the opposite of what a custom reason does; it is the Manual row cause that is deleted on owner change.
Option D (additional criteria for Criteria-Based Sharing) — sharing reasons have nothing to do with criteria-based sharing rules.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers has Controlled by Parent sharing settings on the Contact object and Public Read Only sharing settings on Account, Opportunity, and Case objects. Which two options can the user see while adding Account team members to the Account?
optionA: Case Access
optionB: Opportunity Access
optionC: Contact Access
optionD: Activity Access
explanation:
Case Access and Opportunity Access are the two options the user can see. When adding Account team members, access levels appear for child objects whose OWD is more restrictive than Public Read/Write, and here Case and Opportunity are Public Read Only so their access levels are shown.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Contact Access) — Contact is Controlled by Parent, so it has no independent access setting to show.
Option D (Activity Access) — Activity is not an account-team access option.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Container is creating a custom VF page to allow user to edit contact records. The developer has used an apex:outputField for the Phone field on the contact obj. What is the expected behavior if a user without FLS accesses the VF page?
optionA: The user encounters an error while saving the record
optionB: The field is automatically removed from the page
optionC: The output field is visible to user
optionD: The user is able to enter a value into the phone field
explanation:
The field is automatically removed from the page. An apex:outputField automatically enforces Field-Level Security, so a user without access to the Phone field simply does not see it; Visualforce removes the field rather than throwing an error.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an error while saving the record) — no error occurs; the field is silently omitted and never submitted.
Option C (The output field is visible to user) — FLS is enforced, so the field is hidden.
Option D (able to enter a value into the phone field) — an outputField is display-only, and this one is not rendered at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.securityImplGuide.meta/securityImplGuide/review_and_certification.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_field_perms.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) service reps are assigned to a profile which has View All on the Case object (Private OWD). To make sure service reps have access to all relevant information to attend to customer requests, which two details should Salesforce Architects consider? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Service reps will be able to access all UC contact records if they are controlled by parent.
optionB: Service reps will not be able to access all UC contact records if they are controlled by parent.
optionC: Service reps will be able to access all the UC Account records due to Implicit Sharing.
optionD: Service reps will not be able to access all the UC Account records because Account OWD is private.
explanation:
Service reps not being able to access all UC contact records if they are controlled by parent, and not being able to access all UC Account records because Account OWD is private, are the two details to consider. View All on Case opens up cases and nothing else, and the detail that decides this item is a documented exception to implicit sharing. Salesforce grants read-only access to a parent account to a user who has access to a child case, contact or opportunity — but the same table lists among that behaviour's conditions: "Not granted by the View All permission on the child object."
So the service reps see every case, and still see no accounts, because the Account org-wide default is Private and their case access came from a permission rather than from sharing. Contacts controlled by their parent inherit the account's access, so those stay invisible too.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (able to access all contact records if controlled by parent) — contacts inherit the account's access, and the reps have no account access.
Option C (able to access all Account records due to Implicit Sharing) — sounds like the standard implicit-sharing rule, but implicit parent access is exactly what View All on the child does not trigger.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_implicit_sharing.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_view_all_mod_all.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: For the Universal Containers Commercial and Consumer support departments, having access to Activities for Contacts with which they interact is important. Commercial support users should not see Consumer Accounts/Contacts and Consumer support users should not see Commercial Accounts/Contacts. Assuming the Organization-Wide Default for Activities is set to "Controlled by Parent", what is the minimum level of Sharing access a support user would need to Accounts/Contacts to view associated Activities?
optionA: Private Account/Contact Sharing Default with a Sharing Rule for each department set to Public Read/Write access to Accounts/Contacts.
optionB: Private Account/Contact Sharing Default with a Sharing Rule for each department set to Private access to Accounts/Contacts.
optionC: The users need no access to Accounts/Contacts with the proper Activity Sharing Rules and Profile Permissions for the Accounts Tab.
optionD: Private Account/Contact Sharing Default with a Sharing Rule for each department set to Public Read only access to Accounts/Contacts.
explanation:
Private Account/Contact Sharing Default with a Sharing Rule for each department set to Public Read only is the minimum level. With Activities set to Controlled by Parent, a user needs at least Read on the parent Account or Contact to see its activities, so keep Accounts and Contacts Private and grant each department Read-only through sharing rules to keep commercial and consumer data separated.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (sharing rules set to Public Read/Write) — over-grants; read is enough to see the activities.
Option B (sharing rules set to Private access) — a sharing rule cannot grant "Private"; that is no grant at all, and the users would see nothing.
Option C (no access to Accounts/Contacts, with Activity sharing rules and tab permissions) — Controlled-by-Parent activity visibility cannot be satisfied without access to the parent record, and Activities have no sharing rules of their own.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.managing_the_sharing_model.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: The Architect at Universal Containers has created a List View to show all open Opportunities that were created in the last month, and would like to make this list view visible to certain groups of users. Which two options are available to the Architect for sharing the List View?
optionA: Public Groups
optionB: Profiles
optionC: Roles and Subordinates
optionD: Manual Sharing
explanation:
Public Groups and Roles and Subordinates are the two options available for sharing the List View; both scope visibility to a defined set of users.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Profiles) — list views cannot be shared to profiles.
Option D (Manual Sharing) — manual sharing is a per-record mechanism and does not apply to list views.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387584&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.user_groups.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal containers (UC) implemented a private organization-wide default for the Container and Case objects. How can UC give support representatives access to Container and Case records owned by Customer Community users?
optionA: Create an ownership-based sharing rule that gives access to the head of support role and internal subordinates
optionB: Create a criteria-based sharing rule that gives access to the head of support role and internal subordinates
optionC: Support representatives will automatically get access to these records via the role hierarchy.
optionD: Create a Share Group based on the sharing set created for the Customer Community User Profile.
explanation:
Creating a Share Group based on the sharing set created for the Customer Community User Profile is how UC gives support reps access. Records owned by high-volume Customer Community users are not accessible to internal users by default, so a Share Group on that profile's Sharing Set grants internal support reps access to those community-owned Container and Case records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an ownership-based sharing rule to the head of support role) — sharing rules do not reach records owned by high-volume community users, who have no role to be the source of a rule.
Option B (a criteria-based sharing rule to the head of support role) — the same limitation; records owned by high-volume site users are outside sharing-rule reach.
Option C (automatic access via the role hierarchy) — high-volume community users have no role, so nothing rolls up to internal users.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_sharing_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Sales Cloud. During the last quarter of the financial year, they requested a solution in Salesforce to allow them to specify an assistance agent on the opportunity via an assistant field. The system should automatically remove access from the previous assistant when the field changes. What is the optimum solution to meet the requirements?
optionA: Use share group to share opportunities with the assistant agent.
optionB: Use opportunity team and create an assistant field, use apex to share opportunities with the assistant
optionC: Use sharing rule to share opportunities with the assistant agent.
optionD: Use apex sharing to share and unicast opportunities with the assistant agent.
explanation:
Using Apex sharing to share, and unshare, opportunities with the assistant agent is the optimum solution. The requirement is to set an assistant on the opportunity and automatically remove the previous assistant's access when the field changes, and Apex managed sharing is the only option that can both grant the new assistant's share and programmatically delete the prior one. The source question text was garbled, so this is a best-guess reconstruction.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a share group) — share groups share records owned by high-volume site users with internal users; they have nothing to do with an assistant field.
Option B (opportunity team plus Apex to share with the assistant) — the source's answer, but team membership does not auto-remove the prior member on a field change, and if Apex is doing the sharing anyway the team adds nothing.
Option C (a sharing rule to share opportunities with the assistant) — a static rule cannot target a per-record user or revoke access when the field changes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Which two options are available to share a Report or Dashboard folder with other users in the Organization? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Profiles
optionB: Public Groups
optionC: Roles
optionD: Teams
explanation:
Public Groups and Roles are the two options available for sharing a Report or Dashboard folder, among other targets such as individual users and roles and subordinates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Profiles) — not a valid folder-sharing target.
Option D (Teams) — account and opportunity teams are not a folder-sharing target.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.access_report_folders.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is implementing a community of High-Volume Community users. Community users should be able to see records associated to their Account or Contact record. The Architect is planning to use a Sharing Set to provide access to the records. When setting up the Sharing Set, certain objects are not available in the list of Available Objects. Which two reasons explain why an object is excluded from the list of Available Objects in a Sharing Set?
optionA: The object is a custom object, and therefore not available for a sharing set.
optionB: The object's Organization-Wide sharing setting is set to Public Read/Write.
optionC: The object's Organization-Wide sharing setting is set to Private.
optionD: The custom object does not have a lookup to Accounts or Contacts.
explanation:
The object's Organization-Wide sharing setting being Public Read/Write, and the custom object not having a lookup to Accounts or Contacts, are the two reasons. The sharing-set setup page names its own exclusions, and they are exactly the two keyed options: "The Available Objects list excludes: Objects with an org-wide sharing setting of Public Read/Write" and "Custom objects that don't have an account or contact lookup field."
Both exclusions follow from what a sharing set does. It grants site users access to records associated with the account or contact that matches their own, so a custom object with no account or contact lookup gives the access mapping nothing to follow; and an object already open to everyone has no access left to grant.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (custom objects are not available for a sharing set) — custom objects as a class are not excluded; they appear in the supported list.
Option C (the object's OWD is Private) — Private is the setting sharing sets exist to extend, not a disqualifier.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.networks_setting_light_users.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a requirement to expose a web service to their business partners. The web service will be used to allow each business partner to query UC's Salesforce instance to retrieve the status of orders. The business partner should only be allowed access to orders for which the business partner is the fulfillment vendor. The Architect does not want the business partners to utilize the standard APIs and would prefer a custom API be developed. Which three design elements should the Architect consider in order to ensure the data security of the solution? Choose 3 answers.
optionA: Query the Orders object with Dynamic SOQL based upon the fulfillment ID.
optionB: Set the Orders object's sharing settings to Private in the Org-Wide Defaults
optionC: Provide each partner with their own Salesforce login set to API Enabled on the profile.
optionD: Develop a custom Apex web service with a fulfillment ID input attribute
optionE: Develop a custom Apex web service using the "With Sharing" keyword.
explanation:
Querying the Orders object with Dynamic SOQL based on the fulfillment ID, setting the Orders object's sharing to Private, and developing the custom Apex web service with the "With Sharing" keyword are the three design elements. Data security for the partner web service comes from a Private Orders OWD, a "with sharing" Apex service that respects the running user's access, and filtering the SOQL by the partner's fulfillment ID.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (a Salesforce login per partner with API Enabled) — a login is how the partner authenticates, not a row-level security design element; on its own it enforces nothing about which orders are returned.
Option D (a custom Apex web service with a fulfillment ID input attribute) — an input parameter supplied by the caller can be spoofed; it does not itself enforce row-level security.

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has Public Read Only sharing settings on the Opportunity object. What Opportunity access options can the user see while adding account team members to the Account?
optionA: Read Only
optionB: Private and Read Only
optionC: Private
optionD: Read Only and Read/Write
explanation:
Read Only and Read/Write are the Opportunity access options the user can see. When the Opportunity OWD is Public Read Only, the account-team Opportunity access dropdown offers only the levels at or above that baseline.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Read Only) — incomplete: Read/Write is offered too.
Option B (Private and Read Only) — Private is not selectable, because team access cannot drop below the OWD.
Option C (Private) — likewise not offered; the OWD already grants read to everyone.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.accountteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has the following requirements: A custom Loan object requires Org-Wide Defaults set to Private. The owner of the Loan record will be the Loan Origination Officer. The Loan record must be shared with a specific Underwriter on a loan-by-loan basis. The Underwriters should only see the Loan records for which they are assigned. What should the Architect recommend to meet these requirements?
optionA: Use criteria-based sharing rules to share the Loan object with the Underwriter based upon the criteria defined in the criteria-based sharing
optionB: Create a lookup relationship from the Loan object to the User object. Use a trigger on the Loan object to create the corresponding record in the Loan share object
optionC: Create a master-detail relationship from the Loan to the User object. Loan records will be automatically shared with the Underwriter
optionD: Create an Apex Sharing Reason on the Loan object that shares the Loan with the Underwriter based upon the criteria defined in the Sharing Reason
explanation:
Creating a lookup relationship from the Loan object to the User object and using a trigger on Loan to create the corresponding Loan share record is the recommendation. Per-loan assignment to a specific underwriter, who is an arbitrary user, requires Apex managed sharing: the User lookup identifies the underwriter and the trigger inserts the share row for them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (criteria-based sharing rules to the Underwriter) — a rule cannot target an arbitrary per-record user; it shares to fixed roles and groups.
Option C (a master-detail relationship from Loan to User) — master-detail to User is not allowed, and it would not share the record with the related user anyway.
Option D (an Apex Sharing Reason that shares based on criteria) — a sharing reason only labels share rows; it contains no criteria and creates no shares by itself.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) implemented Sales Cloud and requested that only certain branch staff trained to sell high risk products can create opportunities for high risk products. In which two ways can an Architect allow only specific branch staff to sell high risk products? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Set Price Book Organization Wide Default to View Only and share the price book (High Risk) with the trained staff.
optionB: Configure Price Book Organization wide default to No Access.
optionC: Share (High Risk) price book with the trained staff via manual sharing.
optionD: Share (High Risk) price book with the trained staff via sharing rule.
explanation:
Setting the Price Book Organization Wide Default to View Only and sharing the High Risk price book with the trained staff, and sharing the High Risk price book with them via manual sharing, are the two ways. Access to sell specific products is controlled through price book sharing: set the Price Book OWD to View Only so not everyone gets the High Risk book, then share that book with the trained staff.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Configure Price Book OWD to No Access) — breaks all price book use for everyone, including the standard book, rather than restricting one book.
Option D (share the High Risk price book via sharing rule) — price books cannot be shared through sharing rules; the mechanism is manual sharing from the price book record.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.products_sharing.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: In order to allow community users to collaborate on Opportunities, which license type must the users.
optionA: Sales Community
optionB: Customer Community
optionC: Partner Community
optionD: Customer Community plus
explanation:
Partner Community is the license type required. Collaborating on Opportunities requires a license that supports the Opportunity object together with roles, which is Partner Community.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales Community) — not a Salesforce license type.
Option B (Customer Community) — oriented to support and self-service; no roles and no Opportunity access.
Option D (Customer Community plus) — adds roles and reporting for customers but does not provide partner opportunity collaboration.

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a custom Visualforce page to display shipment tracking information (custom object, private OWD) to field manager and agents. The IT team wants to make sure that users have access to only the information that is allowed. Which Apex method must be used to make sure only allowed fields are shown to the users?
optionA: isReadable()
optionB: isShowable()
optionC: isAccessible()
optionD: isViewable()
explanation:
isAccessible() is the Apex method to use. To ensure only permitted fields display on a Visualforce or Apex page, call DescribeFieldResult.isAccessible() to check field-level read access before rendering each field.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (isReadable()) — not a Schema describe method.
Option B (isShowable()) — not a Schema describe method.
Option D (isViewable()) — not a Schema describe method; the field-level read check is isAccessible().

https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_perms_enforcing.htm

question: Which two objects support creating queues? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Account.
optionB: Opportunity.
optionC: Lead.
optionD: Case.
explanation:
Lead and Case are the two objects that support queues, among a few others such as custom objects and Orders.

Option A (Account) — accounts do not support queues.
Option B (Opportunity) — opportunities do not support queues.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.users_queue_membership_list.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a Private Sharing Model and restrictive data access settings in place. The data governance team is planning to deploy a master data management tool that will need write access to all system data, and the Architect has been asked to prepare a Data Governance User Profile that has full access to all data regardless of Sharing and CRUD Settings. What is the optimal way to enable this requirement?
optionA: Ensure the profile has the "Modify All Data permission enabled
optionB: Create a Sharing Rule for required Objects, on an API Only profile
optionC: Create an All-Data Access app as a default for this Profile.
optionD: Enable the "Edit Read-Only Fields" permission for this Profile.
explanation:
Ensuring the profile has the "Modify All Data" permission enabled is the optimal way. A profile that needs full read and write access to all data regardless of sharing and CRUD is granted Modify All Data, which bypasses sharing and object-level permissions.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a Sharing Rule for required Objects on an API Only profile) — sharing rules extend record access but do not bypass CRUD, and they would have to be maintained per object.
Option C (an All-Data Access app as a default for the Profile) — an app is a navigation container; it grants no data access.
Option D (the "Edit Read-Only Fields" permission) — lets a user edit fields marked read-only on a layout; it does not grant universal data access.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.users_profiles_view_all_mod_all.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Mary is Joe's manager in the role hierarchy. The OWD for a custom Invoice object is Public ReadOnly and Mary's profile is not granted the Read permission for the Invoice object. What action can Mary take on Joe's Invoice records?
optionA: Read/Write
optionB: Edit Only
optionC: None
optionD: View Only
explanation:
None is the action Mary can take on Joe's Invoice records. The OWD is Public Read Only, but Mary's profile lacks Read on the Invoice object, and object-level CRUD gates everything, so the Role Hierarchy cannot grant access to an object she has no permission for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Read/Write) — neither the OWD nor the hierarchy grants write, and without object Read she cannot even open the records.
Option B (Edit Only) — there is no such access level, and object permission is missing anyway.
Option D (View Only) — the Public Read Only OWD would give this to a user with object Read; Mary's profile withholds it.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is the best practice for testing sharing and visibility changes?
optionA: Use Administrative and User reports to view the Active Users.
optionB: Use the Login As feature for a sample user in each role and profile.
optionC: Use Field Audit Trail to audit the field meta-data and visibility.
optionD: Use the Sharing button to test Profile and Permission set changes.
explanation:
Using the Login As feature for a sample user in each role and profile is the best practice. Verifying sharing and visibility changes means confirming what a representative user can actually see.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Administrative and User reports to view the Active Users) — lists who is active; it says nothing about what they can see.
Option C (Field Audit Trail to audit field meta-data and visibility) — tracks field value history, not who can see records.
Option D (the Sharing button to test Profile and Permission set changes) — the Sharing button shows record shares on one record; it does not exercise profile or permission-set changes.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.logging_in_as_another_user.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a custom object to track the internal net promoter score (NPS) for all .. How can UC ensure that NPS records cannot be accessed by an individual employee's manager?
optionA: Create a criteria-based sharing rule to remove access to Manager role and above in the Role ..
optionB: Remove Create, Read, Edit and Delete from Manager Profiles and Permission sets.
optionC: Use Apex Sharing to remove NPS object share records for Manager profiles.
optionD: Set organization wide default to Private and uncheck the Access Using Hierarchies option for the NPS object
explanation:
Setting the organization wide default to Private and unchecking the Access Using Hierarchies option for the NPS object is how UC ensures managers cannot see NPS records. With the object Private and hierarchy inheritance disabled, managers do not inherit their subordinates' records.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a criteria-based sharing rule to remove access from the Manager role and above) — sharing rules only grant access; there is no rule that removes it.
Option B (Remove Create, Read, Edit and Delete from Manager profiles and permission sets) — would block managers from every NPS record, including any they legitimately own or are given.
Option C (Apex Sharing to remove NPS share records for Manager profiles) — hierarchy access is not stored as share rows that Apex could delete; it is computed, so there is nothing to remove.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_owd_about.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: To grant Universal Containers sales managers access to shipment records it was necessary to leverage Apex managed sharing, and the IT team is worried about improper access to records. Which two features and best practices should a Salesforce architect recommend to mitigate the risk?
optionA: Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility will be followed.
optionB: Use runAs system method in test classes to test using different users and profiles.
optionC: Use with Sharing keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility will be followed
optionD: Use isAccessible keyword in Apex classes to assure record visibility will be followed.
explanation:
Using the runAs system method in test classes to test different users and profiles, and using the with sharing keyword in Apex classes so record visibility is followed, are the two features and best practices. Apex managed sharing is created by code running in system context, so the two safeguards are one that re-imposes the running user's visibility and one that proves it. Declaring the class with sharing does the first: Understanding Sharing notes that a trigger started from a class that is not defined with the keyword "runs in system mode" and so "doesn't require the running user to have specific access". Testing with runAs does the second - inside a runAs block "the user's sharing rules and object-level and field-level permissions are enforced... regardless of the sharing mode (with sharing or without sharing) of the test class", so a test can demonstrate what each profile actually sees.
Be precise about why the other two fail, because they are not equally imaginary.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Use isShareable keyword in Apex classes) — there is no isShareable member on Apex's Schema.DescribeSObjectResult, so the option names nothing at all.
Option D (Use isAccessible keyword in Apex classes) — isAccessible() is real, documented as returning "true if the current user can see this object", but it is a describe method reporting object-level access, not a keyword, and it says nothing about which individual records a user may see.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_security_sharing_rules.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_tools_runas.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_bulk_sharing_understanding.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_methods_system_sobject_describe.htm

question: Which users have access to Opportunity records owned by an external user, assuming no other changes to the sharing model have been implemented?
optionA: The record owner and any user above the external user in the role hierarchy.
optionB: The record owner only.
optionC: The record owner and any user below the external user in the role hierarchy.
optionD: The record owner and all internal users.
explanation:
The record owner and any user above the external user in the role hierarchy have access. An opportunity owned by an external (community) user is, by default, visible to that owner and to internal users above the external user's role in the hierarchy, because the role hierarchy rolls access upward.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (The record owner only) — the hierarchy above the partner account's roles still grants access upward.
Option C (The record owner and any user below the external user) — access never flows down the hierarchy.
Option D (The record owner and all internal users) — only the internal users above the external user's role, not every internal user, gain access.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.networks_partner_roles_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_controlling_access_using_hierarchies.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is updating its Organization-Wide Sharing Settings for the Account Object from a "Public Read/Write" model to a "Private" model, so that they can hide certain national accounts from sales reps and sales managers. These national accounts should only be accessible by sales directors and above. Universal Container's Role Hierarchy matches its organizational hierarchy. Which two options should the Architect consider when designing the solution? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Sales directors will need a sharing rule created so that they can see accounts owned by Sales Users.
optionB: National accounts must be owned by a user who is above the sales managers in the Role Hierarchy.
optionC: Apex managed sharing will have to be disabled for the account object to protect the national accounts.
optionD: If a sales rep is added to the Opportunity Team for a national account, they will gain access to account data.
explanation:
National accounts being owned by a user above the sales managers in the Role Hierarchy, and a sales rep added to a national account's Opportunity Team gaining access to account data, are the two options to consider. Under a Private model the accounts must be owned above the managers so the managers do not inherit them, and the side effect to note is that Opportunity Team membership grants implicit access to the parent account.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Sales directors will need a sharing rule to see accounts owned by Sales Users) — the hierarchy already handles it; directors above the reps inherit their accounts.
Option C (Apex managed sharing will have to be disabled) — Apex managed sharing is not in use here and cannot be "disabled" for an object; it is irrelevant to protecting the national accounts.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_implicit_sharing.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.salesteam_def.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has junction object called "Job Production Facility", with 2 master-detail relationships to the Job and Production Facility custom objects. Both master records have a private sharing model. What statement is true if a user's profile allows access (Create/Read) to the Job, but no access to the Production Facility Object?
optionA: The user will be granted read access to the Production Facility record
optionB: The user will see the junction object and the link to the Production Facility.
optionC: The user will see the junction object but not the link to the Production Facility.
optionD: The user will not be able to see the junction object records or the field values.
explanation:
The user will not be able to see the junction object records or the field values. Custom Object Security states the rule for junction objects directly. For an object on the detail side of a master-detail relationship, viewing a record requires "Read permission and read access to the related master record. If the record has two master records in a many-to-many relationship, the user must have read access to both master records."
This user has no access to Production Facility at all, so the second condition fails and the junction records are invisible — not partially visible, and not visible minus a link. Detail records also inherit their security from their masters and cannot be permissioned independently, so there is no way to grant the junction on its own.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (granted read access to the Production Facility record) — access never flows upward from a junction; seeing a junction record would not have granted read on the parent, even in the case where the user could see the junction.
Option B (sees the junction object and the link to the Production Facility) — the junction record itself is invisible when either master is inaccessible.
Option C (sees the junction object but not the link) — there is no partial rendering; the record is withheld entirely.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.dev_security.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.relationships_manytomany.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A developer at Universal Container is building an integration within a managed package for their internal org that requires login to an external system. The end point requires basic authentication. The Architect would like to ensure that the username and password are managed securely. Which three options should the Architect recommend to secure the credentials?
optionA: Store the credentials in a custom object using encrypted fields
optionB: Store the credentials in named credentials that are used in the apex callout
optionC: Store the credentials in the apex code, which will not be available to non-admins
optionD: Store the credentials in protected custom metadata that are used in the apex callout
optionE: Store the credentials in protected custom settings that are used in the apex callout
explanation:
Storing the credentials in named credentials, in protected custom metadata, or in protected custom settings used in the Apex callout are the three options to recommend. Named credentials store and inject the credentials securely, and protected custom metadata or protected custom settings in a managed package cannot be viewed by subscribers.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a custom object using encrypted fields) — an encrypted field is readable by anyone granted View Encrypted Data in the subscriber org, so it is not secure storage for callout credentials.
Option C (in the Apex code, not available to non-admins) — hard-coded credentials ship with the package and cannot be rotated; "not available to non-admins" is not a security boundary.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.cs_schema_settings.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.custommetadatatypes_package_access.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Sales managers want their team members to help each other close Opportunities. The Opportunity and Account organization-wide defaults are private. To grant Opportunity access to sales reps on the same team, ownership-based sharing rules were created for each team. What is the side effect of this approach?
optionA: All sales reps will have Read access to Accounts for all Opportunities.
optionB: Sales Reps on the same team will have Edit access to the Accounts for Opportunities owned by then team members.
optionC: Sales reps on the same team will have Read access to the Accounts for Opportunities owned by their team members.
optionD: All sales reps will have Read access to all Accounts.
explanation:
Sales reps on the same team having Read access to the Accounts for Opportunities owned by their team members is the side effect. Ownership-based opportunity sharing rules grant implicit Read access to the parent Account of those opportunities, so team members get Read, not Edit, on those specific accounts rather than on all accounts.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (All sales reps will have Read access to Accounts for all Opportunities) — the rules are per team, so the implicit account access is limited to each team's opportunities.
Option B (Edit access to the Accounts for team members' Opportunities) — implicit parent sharing grants Read only, never Edit.
Option D (All sales reps will have Read access to all Accounts) — no rule shares accounts at all; the implicit access covers only the parents of shared opportunities.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.draes.meta/draes/draes_object_relationships_implicit_sharing.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.security_sharing_rules_owner.htm&type=5&language=en_US

question: The architect at Universal Containers would like to prevent users from editing encrypted fields. Assuming no customizations are implemented, which two options should the Architect choose to support the requirement? Choose 2 answers.
optionA: Validation Rules
optionB: Page Layout settings
optionC: Apex Triggers
optionD: Workflow Rules
explanation:
Validation Rules and Page Layout settings are the two options. Without custom code, you prevent editing of encrypted fields by using a validation rule that blocks changes or by setting the field to read-only on the page layout.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Apex Triggers) — code, which the stem rules out as a customization.
Option D (Workflow Rules) — act after the record is saved rather than preventing the edit.

https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.fields_about_encrypted_fields.htm&language=en_US&type=5
